AWS WAF Managed Rules — AWS Colors Rules Set (CRS), which automatically includes protection against sqlmap and other known attack tools without manual configuration
questions.explanation: Correct. AWS WAF supports string matching rules ('String match rules') with the options: header, query string, body, etc.), header name ('User-Agent'), and type of match ('Contains', 'Exactly matches', 'Starts with', 'Ends with', 'Regex'). A string match rule with 'Contains' in 'User-Agent' for 'sqlmap' will block any request with that string in the User-Agent header.
questions.hint: Think about the type of rule WAF inspecting the content of a header HTTP specific in search of a matching string — what type of match you use?
optionRationales: Correct. AWS WAF supports string matching rules ('String match rules') with the options: header, query string, body, etc.), header name ('User-Agent'), and type of match ('Contains', 'Exactly matches', 'Starts with', 'Ends with', 'Regex'). A string match rule with 'Contains' in 'User-Agent' for 'sqlmap' will block any request with that string in the User-Agent header.

Incorrect. IP-based rate-based rules count IP requests over time — do not inspect header content HTTP A striker who uses sqlmap could do 1 requisitioning each different IP (IPs/botnets rotation) and bypass the rate-based rule without ever reaching the thread.

Incorrect. SQL injection match rules no WAF analyze the VALORES of fields (query strings, body, headers) in search of SINTAXE of SQL injection (ex.: SELECT, UNION, DROP TABLE) — they don't identify the FERRAMENTA used by name (e.g. 'sqlmap' in User-Agent). To block by tool name in User-Agent, string match rule is the correct type.

Partially correct but imprecise. AWS Colors Rules Set (CRS) and other managed rules include protections against attack patterns (SQL injection, XSS), but do not necessarily identify all the specific tools by name in the User-Agent. For an explicit rule that blocks 'sqlmap' in the User-Agent, a custom string match rule is more accurate and guaranteed than depending on CRS.

questions.text: A team developed a function Lambda that accesses a pocket S3 in OUTRA count AWS. The function uses one IAM Role with the right policy for sts:AssumeRole on cross-account roll, and the cross-account roll has permissions s3:GetObject for the bucket. However, the call fails with 'Access Denied'. The bucket policy of the bucket has no explicit configuration for the cross-account roll. What is the most likely cause?
options: The function Lambda you need to have one VPN or Direct Connect with destination account for which calls S3 cross-account run with assumed credentials
A IAM Destination role (cross-account) cannot have permissions s3:GetObject to your own account — cross-account roles can only access resources in other accounts
The problem is that the function Lambda use one IAM Role, not a user IAM — o S3 only accept user cross-account access IAM with key accesses, not of temporary roles

When cross-account credentials assumed are used to access S3, the bucket on the account of DESTINO it needs to have an explicit loop policy granting access to the cross-account roll — unlike intra-account access, where the IAM Roll policy is enough.
questions.explanation: That's a fundamental behavior of the S3 for cross-account access: when a OUTRA tells access to a pocket, the IAM policy of identity in the account of origin is necessary but NOT enough — the pocket in the account of DESTINO it also needs a resource-based policy that explicitly authorizes cross-account identity access. Without the money policy in the destination account, the S3 denies access even if the IAM policy in the account of origin allows.
questions.hint: For access S3 DENTRO of the same account, IAM Roller policy is enough. S3 CROSS-ACCOUNT, what changes in the assessment of permissions of the S3?
optionRationales: That's a fundamental behavior of the S3 for cross-account access: when a OUTRA tells access to a pocket, the IAM policy of identity in the account of origin is necessary but NOT enough — the pocket in the account of DESTINO it also needs a resource-based policy that explicitly authorizes cross-account identity access. Without the money policy in the destination account, the S3 denies access even if the IAM policy in the account of origin allows.

Incorrect. S3 Cross-account via assumed credentials (STS) are made via the public endpoint of the S3 (HTTPS) — do not require private network connectivity as VPN or Direct Connect. The problem is of AUTHORIZATION (lack of bucket policy in the destination account), not network connectivity.

Incorrect. There is no such restriction — a IAM Role in any account may have permissions to resources in the same account or in other accounts. The problem described is of authorization of the LADO DO BUCKET (absence of bucket policy), not a limitation of the type of permission that the roll may have.

Incorrect. S3 accepts cross-account access both from users IAM the roles — the temporary credentials obtained via AssumeRole are fully supported for access to the S3 (and all services AWS). There is no such distinction between users and roles for cross-account access to S3.

questions.text: An application uses the Amazon RDS with Multi-AZ enabled. During a failover test, the team realized that the bank's endpoint returned errors by about 60-120 seconds before application automatically reconnect. The architecture has connection pooling (without RDS Proxy) and the application tries to reconnect with immediate retry. RDS Multi-AZ did not completely eliminate downtime in this scenario?
options: The RDS Multi-AZ provides only storage redundancy — doesn't do automatic computer failure; it's the Read Replica that provides instance failure
Multi-AZ failed because the standby instance was in a different AZ — applications in Multi-AZ need to be in the same AZ as the primary for seamless connection

The failover of RDS Multi-AZ requires a DNS TTL Flip — after promotion of the standby instance, the DNS of the endpoint delay between 60-120 seconds to propagate, period during which the application with TTL of DNS cached still points to the endpoint of the inactive primary instance
The failover team of the RDS Multi-AZ is of only 10-20 seconds; the 60-120 observed seconds indicate a bug in the application that does not release connections TCP old before trying to reconnect
questions.explanation: Correct. RDS Multi-AZ makes automatic failover by updating the log DNS of the endpoint to point to the standby instance promoted. The downtime time observed corresponds to the propagation of the TTL of DNS (usually 60(s) added to the standby promotion time (~20-30s). To minimize, the application should use TTL of DNS low and ideally, RDS Proxy (which maintains a pool of connections and handles the failover transparently).
questions.hint: Multi-AZ uses DNS to fail — what happens to the TTL of record DNS during the transition to the standby instance?
optionRationales: Correct. RDS Multi-AZ makes automatic failover by updating the log DNS of the endpoint to point to the standby instance promoted. The downtime time observed corresponds to the propagation of the TTL of DNS (usually 60(s) added to the standby promotion time (~20-30s). To minimize, the application should use TTL of DNS low and ideally, RDS Proxy (which maintains a pool of connections and handles the failover transparently).

Incorrect. The goal of Multi-AZ is to have standby in a different AZ — that's what ensures availability if primary AZ fails. Applications in any AZ within the region connect via the endpoint DNS of the RDS, which is updated to point to the new primary after failure. The application AZ does not need to correspond to the AZ of the instance. RDS.

Incorrect. RDS Multi-AZ makes FAILOVER AUTOMATICAL instance (computing + storage) — the standy instance is a complete synchronous replica, and in primary failure, the standy is automatically promoted. Read Replicas are asynchronous copies for scalable reading, not automatic failover.

Partially correct in part of the TTL: connections TCP old (TCP keepalive/timeouts) may contribute to the connection latency, but the main factor is the DNS TTL. The claim that the failover is 'only 10-20s' is a simplification — the total process includes failure detection, standby promotion and propagation of DNS, Can take it 1-2 minutes.

questions.text: A company has a critical application that uses Amazon SQS to process e-commerce requests. Over time, the team observed that some requests are processed DUAS VEZES, The row is of the Standard type (no FIFO). What is the root cause of this problem and how to solve it?
options: The problem is the competition of multiple consumers in the same row — each message should be processed by only one specific consumer; use SNS with fanout for multiple dedicated consumers eliminates the dispute

The problem is that the Standard row is not ordered — messages arrive out of order, and the business code interprets out of order orders as duplicate orders; use SQS FIFO ensures ordination and eliminates perceived 'duplicate'

The problem is the very short visibility timeout — if the consumer function takes longer than the visibility timeout to process, the message becomes visible again in the queue to another consumer; increasing visibility timeout solves double processing

Rows SQS Standard guarantee delivery 'at-last-once' (at least once), not 'exactly-once' — messages can be delivered more than once. The solution is to use SQS FIFO for processing of orders (guarantee exactly-once within the group), or implement the consumer's own power (checking if the order has already been processed before executing the order).)
questions.explanation: Right. SQS Standard deliver 'at-last-once' by design — messages can be delivered more than once in rare cases (distributed storage redundancy). For e-commerce orders, the solution is: (1) migrate to SQS FIFO (guarantee exactly-once per deduplication ID), or (2) implements power in the consumer (check a table/cache with the order ID before processing). The combination of both is more robust.
questions.hint: What is the guarantee of a row delivery SQS Standard (at-last-once vs. exactly-once), and what native solution of AWS offers exactly-once delivery for messages?
optionRationales: Right. SQS Standard deliver 'at-last-once' by design — messages can be delivered more than once in rare cases (distributed storage redundancy). For e-commerce orders, the solution is: (1) migrate to SQS FIFO (guarantee exactly-once per deduplication ID), or (2) implements power in the consumer (check a table/cache with the order ID before processing). The combination of both is more robust.

Incorrect as a SINGLE cause. An inadequate visibility timeout can contribute to reprocessing (second delivery before ACK), but the statement describes Standard rows that have at-last-once delivery inherent. Furthermore, increasing the visibility timeout only reduces the probability of double delivery by timeout — does not eliminate the possibility, as Standard rows can deliver duplicates for other reasons (delete failure after processing, multiple storage nodes). Idepower or SQS FIFO are the correct solutions.

Incorrect as diagnosis. The statement describes real duplicate collections (processing occurred twice), not false-positive due to lack of ordering. Lack of ordering can cause problems in sequences (e.g. cancel before creating), but not directly duplicates of collection. The real problem is the delivery at-least-once of the Standard row.

Incorrect. Multiple consumers in a row SQS Standard is the standard — visibility timeout manages mutual exclusion (a message is invisible to other consumers while being processed)). SNS + fanout would distribute the message to MULTIPLES consumers simultaneously, worsening the duplicate processing problem.

questions.text: A company needs high availability for a API REST hosted in a region AWS. The team wants to automatically redirect traffic to a contingency region if the primary region becomes unavailable, with time to fail less than 60 seconds. What a combination of services AWS implements this requirement with multi-region automatic failover?
options: Amazon Route 53 with routing policy of Failover (Primary/Secondary) and health checks active at the endpoint of API — when the health check detects failure in the primary region (30-60s), Route 53 automatically resolves the DNS for the secondary region endpoint
AWS Lambda with Event Source Mapping cross-region — Lambda automatically processes secondary region events when primary is unavailable

AWS Global Accelerator with endpoint groups in two regions and health checks — the Global Accelerator detects failure and redirects traffic in seconds via Anycast, without depending on propagation DNS
Amazon CloudFront with Origins in two regions and Origin Failover enabled — CloudFront detect errors HTTP 5xx of primary origin and automatically tries secondary origin in the same request
questions.explanation: Correct.. Route 53 with Failover Routing and health checks is the standard solution for automated multi-region failure. The health check checks the availability of the primary region endpoint at configurable intervals (10s or 30s), and when failure threshold is reached, Route 53 updates answers DNS for the secondary region endpoint — reaching failure within 60-90 seconds (depending on configuration)).
questions.hint: What service does it offer? DNS managed by AWS supports routing policies with automatic failover based on health checks, redirecting between regions when primary failure?
optionRationales: Correct.. Route 53 with Failover Routing and health checks is the standard solution for automated multi-region failure. The health check checks the availability of the primary region endpoint at configurable intervals (10s or 30s), and when failure threshold is reached, Route 53 updates answers DNS for the secondary region endpoint — reaching failure within 60-90 seconds (depending on configuration)).

Correct but not the ONLY correct solution — and the Global Accelerator has even lower failure latency (typically 30(s) use Anycast instead of DNS. Both are valid, but for the question about 'less than' 60 seconds', or Route 53 also responds — Global Accelerator is not the only correct alternative., Route 53 Failover is the most commonly cited solution for this scenario in certification SAA-C03.

Partially correct but for a specific case. CloudFront Origin Failover works for static/cacheable content and can cause failure to a secondary source within the same request in case of error. However, for a API REST dynamic, or CloudFront Origin Failover has limitations (does not work with POST/PUT/DELETE by default) and is not the standard multi-region failure solution. Route 53 with Failover Routing is more suitable for failing from API multi-region.

Incorrect. Lambda Event Source Mapping is not a multi-region failover mechanism of API — It connects Lambda to event sources (SQS, Kinesis, DynamoDB Streams) within a region. There is no automatic mechanism that redirects invocations from API Lambda from one region to another without Route 53 or API Gateway with explicit failover configuration.

questions.text: A team uses Amazon SQS to unplug an image processing application. Some messages repeatedly fail in processing (corrupted images). 3 attempts, these messages are blocking the queue, preventing the processing of subsequent valid messages. SQS solve this problem by isolating problematic messages?
options: Configure a Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) associated with the main row with maxReceiveCount=3 — after 3 processing failures, message is automatically moved to DLQ, where it can be investigated without blocking the main row
Configure a row SQS FIFO instead of Standard — messages in rows FIFO are processed in order and a problematic message blocks only your group of messages, not the whole row
Increase visibility timeout to 24 hours — messages in processing become invisible for longer, giving the code a chance of retry attempts over a whole day before giving up
Enable Server-Side Encryption (SSE) in the row — corrupted messages are automatically discarded by SQS if they do not pass the integrity validation during the description
questions.explanation: That's right. (DLQ) is the mechanism of the SQS to isolate problematic messages. When setting up the redirect policy with maxReceiveCount=3, messages that failed 3 times are automatically moved to the DLQ associated. The main row continues to process valid messages without blocking, and the team can investigate messages in DLQ to understand and correct errors.
questions.hint: What is the functionality of SQS automatically receives messages that have exceeded the maximum number of processing attempts, isolating them from the main row?
optionRationales: That's right. (DLQ) is the mechanism of the SQS to isolate problematic messages. When setting up the redirect policy with maxReceiveCount=3, messages that failed 3 times are automatically moved to the DLQ associated. The main row continues to process valid messages without blocking, and the team can investigate messages in DLQ to understand and correct errors.

Incorrect. Increasing visibility timeout does not solve intrinsically problematic messages (such as corrupted images) — they will continue to fail regardless of how long the application tries. This would only delay the problem without isolating it. DLQ is the correct mechanism for isolating messages that repeatedly fail.

Partially correct about blocking behavior by Message Group ID in rows FIFO, but does not solve the problem of corrupted messages. A corrupted message in a Message Group still blocks that group indefinitely. The correct solution is the DLQ, which can be configured in both Standard and Standard rows FIFO to isolate messages that exceed maxReceiveCount.

Incorrect. SSE encrypts messages at rest for security — has no connection to message content validation (such as corrupted images). Corrupt messages in the CONTENT (invalid data for the application) pass through the validation of the integrity of the SQS no problem — SQS does not understand the business context of content.

questions.text: An application uses Amazon DynamoDB to store session data from users. The application is growing globally and the team wants users in Asia to have low latency when accessing their session data, without session changes made in Asia appearing inconsistent for the same user if he accesses the application from Europe a few seconds later. DynamoDB is more suitable?
options: DynamoDB Global Tables — replicates data between multiple regions automatically with replication latency typically below 1 second (possibly consistency cross-region); for the session scenario, the application can use sticky sessions or route by region of origin of the user to minimize cross-region accesses in the same user
DynamoDB with Read Replicas in multiple regions — replicas of reading in each region serve users locally with low latency for readings, while written go to the master table in the primary region
Amazon ElastiCache for Redis with Redis Cluster Mode Global — Centralizes Redis sessions with replication between regions for low access latency
DynamoDB with Streams and Lambda for custom replication — each change in the primary region, a Lambda replicates data to tables DynamoDB in other regions
questions.explanation: Correct.. DynamoDB Global Tables is the multi-region replication mechanism of DynamoDB — supports readings and writings in each region with asynchronous replication between regions (if any consistency). For user sessions, the cross-region inconsistency problem is usually mitigated via geographic rotation (Route 53) which keeps the user in the same region in most sessions. For cases where this is insufficient, the application can implement session versioning.
questions.hint: What is the functionality of DynamoDB creates replicated tables in multiple regions AWS with the support of E readings written in each region, for globally distributed applications?
optionRationales: Correct.. DynamoDB Global Tables is the multi-region replication mechanism of DynamoDB — supports readings and writings in each region with asynchronous replication between regions (if any consistency). For user sessions, the cross-region inconsistency problem is usually mitigated via geographic rotation (Route 53) which keeps the user in the same region in most sessions. For cases where this is insufficient, the application can implement session versioning.

Incorrect. DynamoDB DO NOT have a separate 'Read Replicas' concept as the RDS. The DynamoDB Global Tables is the multi-region replication mechanism, where each region has a full copy and WRITABLE Table (not just reading)). DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) It's a cache in memory but it's intra-regional..

Incorrect as recommended approach. DynamoDB Streams + Lambda for custom replication is a workable solution that reinvents what Global Tables already offers natively — with lower latency and greater reliability. Lambda, sorting of events, dealing with conflicts) makes this approach inferior to the Global Tables for this case.

Incorrect. Amazon ElastiCache does not support multi-region automatic replication (cross-region) as the DynamoDB Global Tables — ElastiCache is an intra-regional service. For sessions in multiple regions with ElastiCache, a complex customized implementation would be required, which is not the recommended standard.

questions.text: A company operates a web application with Auto Scaling Group (ASG). The team detected that the ASG is making scale-out and scale-in quickly in short cycles (thrashing), adding and removing instances several times an hour, even with stable traffic. This causes impact on users and generates unnecessary cost. What configuration of the ASG helps prevent such behavior?
options: Increase the cooldown period of ASG (standard 300 seconds) — cooldown prevents new scaling activities from starting before the effect of the previous action is fully reflected in metrics, reducing thrashing
Configure the escalator protection in all instances of the ASG — this prevents the ASG remove instances, eliminating the removal and addition cycle
Increase the polling interval of the metrics of CloudWatch for 5 minutes — metrics with a higher interval produce less frequent scaling decisions
Replace the simple scaling policy with Target Tracking Scaling — Target Tracking continuously adjusts the ability to maintain a metric-target, avoiding overshooting that causes thrashing
questions.explanation: Right. The cooldown period doesn't ASG defines how long it should go after a scaling action before another is started. A very short (or standard) cooldown can cause thrashing if metrics don't have time to stabilize after adding/removing instances. Increasing the cooldown gives time for traffic to spread through new instances and metrics to stabilize before a new scaling decision is made..
questions.hint: What parameter in Auto Scaling Group defines a waiting time after each scaling action, during which no new scaling action can be initiated?
optionRationales: Right. The cooldown period doesn't ASG defines how long it should go after a scaling action before another is started. A very short (or standard) cooldown can cause thrashing if metrics don't have time to stabilize after adding/removing instances. Increasing the cooldown gives time for traffic to spread through new instances and metrics to stabilize before a new scaling decision is made..

Target Tracking is an improvement on Simple Scaling, because Target Tracking algorithm is designed to minimize thrashing by making gradual adjustments. However, the statement specifically asks about cooldown as a thrashing prevention mechanism — and cooldown is the configuration directly related to the behavior described. Target Tracking still uses warmup periods (equivalent to cooldown) to mitigate the same problem..

Incorrect. Scale-in protection in TODAS the instances would prevent the ASG to remove instances permanently — the group would always be in the maximum size reached, without dynamic adjustment. This eliminates the scale-in (not thrashing), causing continuous oversupply — the opposite and equally undesirable problem.

Incorrect. Auto Scaling uses metrics of CloudWatch, but has no direct control over the 'polling interval' of metrics for scaling purposes. ASG) and the warmup period are the correct controls for the frequency of scaling decisions. 5 minutes could introduce excessive latency in the scale-out (slower reaction to actual peaks of load).

questions.text: A company uses Amazon RDS PostgreSQL with auto backup enabled (retention of 7 A developer accidentally executed a command DROP TABLE in a table critical to the 14:23 The team needs to recover the data with the least possible impact on production. What is the correct approach?
options: Perform a Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR) for 14:22 (1 minutes before DROP TABLE) restoring to a new instance RDS — examine and export the data from the restored instance table, then import to the production instance, without need to replace the production instance
Enable Multi-AZ retrospectively in the instance — the standby instance was synchronized continuously before DROP TABLE and can be promoted to recover data
Use AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) to make a complete migration from the last snapshot to the production instance, preserving all transactions from the snapshot
Restore the latest automatic snapshot (previous to DROP TABLE) directly on the existing production instance — this will replace the production instance with the previous version of the bank
questions.explanation: Correct. PITR restores the instance to any point in the last 7 days (according to set retention) for a NOVA instance RDS — does not replace the production instance directly. The correct process is: restore to T-1 minute (new instance), export the lost table of the restored instance (pg_dump), import to production (pg_restore). This minimizes the impact because production is not interrupted during restoration.
questions.hint: Remember: PITR restores to one NOVA instance (does not replace production) with granularity of minutes — this allows you to recover specific data from a table without replacing all production.
optionRationales: Correct. PITR restores the instance to any point in the last 7 days (according to set retention) for a NOVA instance RDS — does not replace the production instance directly. The correct process is: restore to T-1 minute (new instance), export the lost table of the restored instance (pg_dump), import to production (pg_restore). This minimizes the impact because production is not interrupted during restoration.

Incorrect for two reasons: (1) Restoring a snapshot DOES NOT replace the existing instance — always creates a NOVA the court; and (2) restoring a daily snapshot would mean losing TODAS transactions since the last automatic snapshot (which may be hours before the DROP TABLE), while the PITR allows you to recover up to 5 minutes before the incident with granularity of minutes.

Incorrect. DMS is a continuous migration tool between different banks or for replication CDC — is not suitable for data recovery within the same bank. DMS has no direct access to snapshots for 'replay' transactions. PITR with new instance + table export is the correct approach.

Incorrect. Multi-AZ uses SYNCRON replication — standby replica TODAS the transactions of the primary, including the DROP TABLE. Promoting standby would result in a bank also without the table, as the deletion has already been replicated. Multi-AZ is for failure of availability (hardware/AZ failure protection), not for protection against logical data errors.

questions.text: A company has an e-commerce application with predictable traffic peaks (Black Friday, Cyber Monday). The team wants to ensure sufficient capacity ANTES of the peak, without depending that the Auto Scaling is reacting to the real-time burden. Auto Scaling implements this proactivity requirement?
options: Step Scaling with low thread (ex.: 30% CPU) — when climbing aggressively before reaching 100% of CPU, o ASG always will have free capacity available during peak
Predictive Scaling — uses Machine Learning to analyze historical traffic patterns and pre-provide capacity automatically before peaks, without manual schedule setting
Target Tracking Scaling with RequestCount metric by Target — or ASG automatically increases before peak based on request forecast

Scheduled Scaling — the pre-set team sets actions to increase the minimum/desirable capacity of the ASG at specific times (e.g., Friday) 23h before Black Friday), ensuring ready instances before peak without metric dependence
questions.explanation: Correct. The Scheduled Scaling of ASG allows for pre-configuration of specific date/hour capacity increases — ideal for predictable peaks such as Black Friday. Capacity is proactively added before peak, without expecting metrics such as CPU/RequestCount reach thresholds. After peak, other scheduled action can reduce capacity.
questions.hint: When peak dates/hours are known in advance (Black Friday), what is the policy ASG allows you to set up exactly QUANDO the capacity should be increased proactively?
optionRationales: Correct. The Scheduled Scaling of ASG allows for pre-configuration of specific date/hour capacity increases — ideal for predictable peaks such as Black Friday. Capacity is proactively added before peak, without expecting metrics such as CPU/RequestCount reach thresholds. After peak, other scheduled action can reduce capacity.

Incorrect in response MAIS Predictive Scaling uses ML to predict and pre-provide based on historical patterns — it is excellent for recurring but unpredictable peaks at exact times. CONHECIDOS (Black Friday), Scheduled Scaling is more reliable and immediate — it doesn't depend on enough data history for prediction, and the team has direct control over when capacity is added.

Incorrect. Target Tracking Scaling is REATIVO — it responds to metrics that are already elevated, does not foresee future peaks. The reactive scale-out takes minutes after the peak start (collection of metrics + time of provisioning of instances), which can cause degradation during the beginning of the peak. The question asks capacity ANTES peak.

Incorrect. Step Scaling with low threshold is still REATIVO — waits for CPU reach 30% in steep peaks (like Black Friday at 00(h), the load may go from 10% for 300% in minutes — reactive Step Scaling may not be able to add fast enough capacity to avoid degradation.

questions.text: A company uses Amazon Kinesis Data Streams for real-time log intake. The team is seeing an increase in the 'ProvisionedThroughputExceedException' error when multiple applications try to read the same shard. What change solves this shard read throughput problem?
options: Migratory to Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose — Firehose has no shard reading throughput limits
Increase the number of shards (Shard Splitting) — with more shards, the total readthroughput increases and the error ProvidedThroughputExceeded is solved

Enable Enhanced Fan-Out no Kinesis Data Streams — With Enhanced Fan-Out, every registered consumer receives 2 MB/s reading by shard via a connection HTTP/2 dedicated (push), without sharing the 2 MB/s standard reading among all shard consumers
Implement polling with exponential backoff in consumer applications — by reducing the frequency of polling, readings are below the limit of 2 MB/s per shard
questions.explanation: Correct. The standard reading limit of Kinesis Data Streams 2 MB/s per shard, shared between TODOS The Enhanced Fan-Out (HTTP/2) gives each registered consumer their own connection with 2 MB/s dedicated to shard, eliminating the sharing gargalo. Ideal when multiple applications need to consume the same shard data.
questions.hint: The Kinesis has two consumption models: standard polling (2 MB/s shared by shard among all consumers) and a dedicated model that gives each consumer its own throughput — which is the second model?
optionRationales: Correct. The standard reading limit of Kinesis Data Streams 2 MB/s per shard, shared between TODOS The Enhanced Fan-Out (HTTP/2) gives each registered consumer their own connection with 2 MB/s dedicated to shard, eliminating the sharing gargalo. Ideal when multiple applications need to consume the same shard data.

Incorrect for this specific problem. Shard Splitting increases the number of shards (and therefore the total stream throughput), but does not solve the problem when MULTIPLES CONSUMIDORES share the 2 MB/s of UM MESMO shard. Increase shards distributes data, but each new shard would still have the same limit of 2 MB/s shared among all consumers. Enhanced Fan-Out solves multiple consumers problem in the same shard.

Incorrect. Kinesis Data Firehose is a data delivery service for destinations (S3, Redshift, OpenSearch) — is not a substitute for Kinesis Data Streams for cases of multiple custom consumers who process data in real time. Besides, Firehose does not eliminate the problem of multiple consumers; the question is about reading the stream, not delivering data.

Incorrect as scalable solution. exponential backoff is a retry technique that temporarily reduces errors, but reduces the actual processing throughput — applications read data slower. For a case where multiple legitimate consumers need real-time reading, Enhanced Fan-Out is the correct solution that increases capacity without compromising processing speed..

questions.text: A company has one Application Load Balancer (ALB) in front of the fora EC2 in one Auto Scaling A developer noticed that when the ALB detects an instance with failure in the health check and starts the deregistration process, still arrive errors 502/503 no ALB for a few seconds. How to avoid these errors while removing an instance?
options: Configure Connection Draining (Deregistration Delay) no ALB Target Group — it defines a period (default) 300s, configurable) during which ALB does not send NOVAS requests to the instance being deregistered, but allows the requests in progress to be completed before removing the instance from the pool
Configure a more aggressive health check in ALB (interval 5s, threshold of 2 failures) — or ALB removes sick instances faster, before they start returning errors

Enable Stickiness (sticky sessions) on ALB — existing sessions continue to be routed to the same instance, preventing users from receiving errors when having their sessions migrated to another instance.
Use AWS Auto Scaling Lifecycle Hooks to pause the scale-in, run one Lambda Waiting 60 seconds, and only then complete the termination — the ALB has time to remove the instance before it is finished
questions.explanation: Correct. Connection Draining (called Deregistration Delay no ALB) does exactly that: when an instance begins to be removed (via Auto Scaling or health check), or ALB stop sending NOVAS requests for it, but waits for the set timeout for existing connections to end gracefully. 502/503 caused by connections being cut abruptly.
questions.hint: What is the functionality of ALB Target Group defines a waiting period during which new requests are not sent to an instance being removed, but existing ones may complete?
optionRationales: Correct. Connection Draining (called Deregistration Delay no ALB) does exactly that: when an instance begins to be removed (via Auto Scaling or health check), or ALB stop sending NOVAS requests for it, but waits for the set timeout for existing connections to end gracefully. 502/503 caused by connections being cut abruptly.

Incorrect for the problem described. More aggressive health checks help to DETECTAR patients earlier, but do not resolve the problem of errors during DEREGISTRATION of a court which Auto Scaling is removing (by scale-in, for example). The instance may be healthy but being removed by ASG — Connection Draining is the mechanism that protects against errors during this process..

Partially correct in concept (Lifecycle Hooks can be used to coordinate graceful closure) but it is a more complex and indirect solution. ALB Target Group is the right and direct mechanism — it ensures that the ALB stop sending traffic to the instance before it is completed, without the need for additional Lifecycle Hooks for this specific case.

Incorrect. Stickiness ensures that a user is routed to MESMA instance in subsequent requests (useful for local session status), but does not solve the problem of errors while removing an instance. In removal, Stickiness causes the ALB need to migrate all sessions glued to that instance — without Connection Draining, these sessions may receive abrupt errors.

questions.text: A company uses Amazon CloudFormation to manage infrastructure. The team made an update on the stack and a change in the configuration of a Auto Scaling Group failed in the middle of the update, leaving the stack in state 'UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED'. What action should the team take to restore the stack to a stable state?
options: Apply a new template with the CloudFormation which explicitly reverses the changes in the problematic update — the CloudFormation apply manual rollback as a successful new update
Delete the entire stack and recreate from scratch with the original template — it's safer than trying to recover a stack in state UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED

Use 'Continue Update Rollback' in the CloudFormation or via API, specifying the features that are blocking the rollback to skip them — this allows the CloudFormation completes the rollback of the resources you can undo, restoring the stack to the state prior to the problematic update
Use CloudFormation Drift Detection to identify out-of-conformity features and manually sync real state with template — this will unlock stack
questions.explanation: Right. UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED occurs when the autorollback itself failed. The solution is 'Continue Update Rollback', which allows you to specify resources to jump during the rollback (e.g. resources that have been deleted externally and no longer exist). After skipping the problematic resources, the CloudFormation complete the rollback to the last known stable state.
questions.hint: When a stack CloudFormation is in UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED, which specific action allows you to try to complete the rollback, with the option of skippar problematic features?
optionRationales: Right. UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED occurs when the autorollback itself failed. The solution is 'Continue Update Rollback', which allows you to specify resources to jump during the rollback (e.g. resources that have been deleted externally and no longer exist). After skipping the problematic resources, the CloudFormation complete the rollback to the last known stable state.

Incorrect as recommended approach. Delete and recreate can result in data loss (stack database) and unnecessary downtime., CloudFormation can fail by deleting the stack if it also has troubleshooting features. 'Continue Update Rollback' is the correct and safe approach to solving UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED.

Incorrect. Drift Detection identifies resources that have been modified outside the CloudFormation (e.g. manual changes in the console), but does not directly resolve the state UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED. The rollback blocking state is not caused by drift — it is caused by failure in the rollback process itself. 'Continue Update Rollback' is the correct mechanism.

Incorrect for state UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED. In this state, the CloudFormation DO NOT accept new updates directly — it is waiting for the existing rollback to be completed. Trying a new update in this state results in error. Only 'Continue Update Rollback' (or 'Delete Stack') are actions available in that state.

questions.text: A company uses Amazon ECS with Fargate to perform microservices. A critical service was unavailable because all their tasks failed and were not restarted. The team verified that the tasks are in status. 'STOPPED' with message 'Essential container exited'. ECS must be configured to ensure that this service automatically recovers from task failures?
options: Use ECS Service (not standalone tasks) with a desired count configured — the ECS Service continuously monitors the number of running tasks and automatically restarts tasks that stop, always keeping the desired task count running
Configure an Application Auto Scaling for the ECS Service with a Target Tracking policy — this ensures that the number of tasks automatically recovers when there are failures
Enable ECS Container Health Check with automatic reset — the ECS restarts the specific container when the health check fails, without needing a Service
Configure a CloudWatch Alarm that monitors the ECS TaskCount and trigger one Lambda to start new tasks when the count falls below expected
questions.explanation: Correct. Tasks ECS created as part of a ECS Service are managed automatically: if a task for (for any reason including 'essential container exited'), the Service Scheduler detects that running count is below the desired count and automatically launches a new replacement task. Standalone Tasks (without Service) do not have this automatic resilience.
questions.hint: What is the construction of ECS continuously manages the task life cycle, always keeping a desired number running and automatically replacing those that fail?
optionRationales: Correct. Tasks ECS created as part of a ECS Service are managed automatically: if a task for (for any reason including 'essential container exited'), the Service Scheduler detects that running count is below the desired count and automatically launches a new replacement task. Standalone Tasks (without Service) do not have this automatic resilience.

Incorrect as a solution for the specific case. Application Auto Scaling for ECS adjusts to ESCALA metric based (CPU, memory, requests/s) — does not manage recovery of failed tasks. Recovery of failed tasks is the responsibility of ECS SERVICE SCHEDULER (desired count), which is an independent mechanism of Auto Scaling.

Incorrect as the main approach. An alarm CloudWatch + Lambda to restart tasks would be a manual re-implementation of the ECS Service Scheduler already does it automatically and in a much more reliable way. This approach has greater latency (CloudWatch alarm has collection period) and more operational complexity.

Incorrect. Container Health Checks no ECS are used to define when a container is 'healthy', but do not guarantee automatic reboot of tasks stopped by 'essential container exited'. != 0), o ECS for TODA the task — restarting only that container is not the standard behavior of Fargate. The ECS Service with desired count is the correct mechanism.

questions.text: A company uses Amazon Route 53 for traffic routing. The team needs to direct 10% from traffic to a new version of an application (canary release) to test with a small fraction of users before full deployment. Route 53 allows this traffic percentage division?
options: Weighted Routing Policy — the team creates two records for the same domain name with different weights (e.g., current version with weight) 90, new version with weight 10), and the Route 53 distributes traffic proportionally to the weights, resulting in ~10% for the new version
Latency-based Routing Policy — users closest to the new version (which is in a different region) receive traffic proportional to latency, resulting in ~10% according to geographical distribution
Geolocation Routing Policy with the region where the new version is deployed receiving users from a specific geographic area that represents ~10% from the user base
Failover Routing Policy with health checks configured to alternate between primary (90%) and secondary (10%) based on availability
questions.explanation: Correct. Weighted Routing Policy no Route 53 allows to distribute traffic between multiple endpoints with proportional weights. Setting up two records (or sets of records) for the same hostname with weights 90 and 10, approximately 10% of requests DNS will solve for the endpoint of the new version. It is the standard mechanism for canary releases and blue/green deployments percentages in Route 53.
questions.hint: What is the policy of routing Route 53 distributes traffic proportionally to configured numerical weights — ideal for canary releases with precise percentage control?
optionRationales: Correct. Weighted Routing Policy no Route 53 allows to distribute traffic between multiple endpoints with proportional weights. Setting up two records (or sets of records) for the same hostname with weights 90 and 10, approximately 10% of requests DNS will solve for the endpoint of the new version. It is the standard mechanism for canary releases and blue/green deployments percentages in Route 53.

Incorrect. Latency-based Routing directs users to the endpoint with less latency (from the perspective of the network AWS for the region) — does not offer traffic division percentage control. The resulting division would depend on where users are geographically, not on a configurable percentage.

Incorrect. Failover Routing is for high availability (100% traffic goes to primary, with failback to secondary only when the primary is unavailable) — does not divide traffic percently. There is no control of 10%/90% in the policy of Failover.

Incorrect. Geolocation Routing directs users based on their geographical location (country, continent) — does not offer traffic percentage control. The division would depend on the actual geographic distribution of users, not on a configurable and reliable percentage of 10%.

questions.text: A company uses Amazon Aurora with multiple Read Replicas in a region. An application of reports makes heavy queries that are affecting the performance of the writing endpoint of Aurora. The team wants to ensure that reading queries are automatically distributed by the Read Replicas without changing the application code to have two different endpoints. Aurora You'll have to work it out.?
options: Use Aurora Reader Endpoint — a unique endpoint that Aurora automatically manage to balance read connections between all available Read Replicas, without the application needing to know the individual endpoints of each replica
Enable Aurora Global Database — the Global Database creates replicas in multiple regions and directs reading queries to the nearest user area automatically

Configure a Application Load Balancer (ALB) in front of the Read Replicas Aurora — o ALB does load balancing of database connections between replicas, without the application needing specific replication endpoints
Use Amazon RDS Proxy for pooling connections — the RDS Proxy maintains pre-established connections with the Read Replicas and automatically distributes read queries between them
questions.explanation: Correct. Aurora provides an Endpoint Reader Cluster that loads automatically between the Read Replicas. The report application connects to this single reading endpoint, and the Aurora distributes the connections between the available replicas. This does not require changes in the application's business logic — just the configuration of which endpoint to use for reading vs. writing.
questions.hint: The Aurora automatically provides a special read-out endpoint that balances connections between available Read Replicas — what is the name of this endpoint?
optionRationales: Correct. Aurora provides an Endpoint Reader Cluster that loads automatically between the Read Replicas. The report application connects to this single reading endpoint, and the Aurora distributes the connections between the available replicas. This does not require changes in the application's business logic — just the configuration of which endpoint to use for reading vs. writing.

Incorrect. ALB operates in Layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS) — does not support database connection routing (using specific protocols such as PostgreSQL wire protocol). Aurora Reader Endpoint or o RDS Proxy are the right mechanisms. ALB is not used for database connection load balancing.

Incorrect in this case. Aurora Global Database is for replication CROSS-REGION (latency <1s between regions) — does not solve the reading distribution between multiple replicas INTRA-REGIONAL The Reader Endpoint of the cluster Aurora is the mechanism to balance readings between replicas in the same region.

Partially correct in that the RDS Proxy can be configured to route reading traffic, but its main function is the connection pooling to reduce connection overload — not the primary mechanism for balancing between Read Replicas. Aurora Reader Endpoint is the native and correct mechanism for distribution of readings between replicas.

questions.text: A company uses AWS Elastic Beanstalk to deploy a web application. The team wants to update the application version without any downtime, keeping the possibility of immediate rollback if the new version has problems. Elastic Beanstalk is more suitable?
options: All at Once — updates all instances simultaneously; if there is a problem, a manual redeploy of the previous version is required, but the update process itself is the fastest

Blue/Green Deployment Elastic Beanstalk — create an identical environment ('green') with the new version, fully test, and then use 'Swap Environment URLs' to instantly switch traffic; the old environment ('blue') is preserved for immediate rollback if necessary

Immutable Deployment — launches new instances in a temporary group with the new version; after confirmed health, replaces the old instances and finishes the temporary ones; rollback is done ending the new instances
Rolling with Additional Batch — implements the new batch version, adding temporary instances to maintain total capacity, ensuring zero downtime during update
questions.explanation: Right. Blue/Green doesn't Elastic Beanstalk maintains two complete environments: blue (current production) and green (new version). After tests in green, Swap Environment URLs instantly changes the CNAMEs — zero downtime. For rollback, just make another swap back. The blue environment remains intact until the confirmation that the green is OK.
questions.hint: What Deployment Strategy Maintains DOIS complete environments (old and new version) simultaneously, allowing instant exchange of URL and immediate rollback to the previous environment?
optionRationales: Right. Blue/Green doesn't Elastic Beanstalk maintains two complete environments: blue (current production) and green (new version). After tests in green, Swap Environment URLs instantly changes the CNAMEs — zero downtime. For rollback, just make another swap back. The blue environment remains intact until the confirmation that the green is OK.

Partially correct over zero downtime, but rollback is NOT immediate. In Rolling with Additional Batch, part of the instances already have the new version when the update is in progress — a rollback requires a new rollback deployment (which also takes time). Blue/Green is superior when immediate rollback is a requirement.

Partially correct over zero downtime, but the rollback of the Immutable may take time depending on the completion process of the new instances. Blue/Green is superior to immediate rollback as it keeps the old environment completely intact and the swap of URL is instantaneous (without the need to launch new instances).

Incorrect. All at Once causes downtime during the update (all instances being updated at the same time). It is the fastest but least suitable strategy for production environments that need zero downtime.

questions.text: A company uses Amazon EventBridge to process events from multiple sources. A rule EventBridge send events to a function Lambda which makes calls to an external database. Occasionally, the bank becomes temporarily unavailable, causing failures in the Lambda. The team wants faulty events to be automatically reprocessed until the bank becomes available. What configuration implements retry with persistent events?
options: Increase function timeout Lambda for 15 minutes — a Lambda will wait longer for the bank to be available during the same invocation, without need of external retry
Configure Amazon SNS as target of rule EventBridge instead of Lambda — o SNS has integrated automatic retry for all destinations and persistent messages until delivery is confirmed
Enable Lambda Power Tuning to increase memory and speed of function — with more CPU, a Lambda process events faster before the bank's retry timeout is reached

Configure Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) in a row SQS as a destination of failure in EventBridge Event Bus, with a retry rule reproducing row events SQS periodically — or use the EventBridge Archive + Replay to retain and resend failed events
questions.explanation: Correct. EventBridge supports automatic retreats for events that failed delivery (up to 24h by default, configurable up to 24h with configurable number of retries). For persistence beyond that, the EventBridge Destinations allows you to configure a row SQS as DLQ for events that have exhausted the retreats. For more flexible replay, the EventBridge Archive + Replay allows you to retain an event stream and reprocess specific intervals.
questions.hint: To persist events that failed and ensure reprocessing, which line service AWS can be configured as Dead Letter Queue of EventBridge, capturing events after exhausted retreats?
optionRationales: Correct. EventBridge supports automatic retreats for events that failed delivery (up to 24h by default, configurable up to 24h with configurable number of retries). For persistence beyond that, the EventBridge Destinations allows you to configure a row SQS as DLQ for events that have exhausted the retreats. For more flexible replay, the EventBridge Archive + Replay allows you to retain an event stream and reprocess specific intervals.

Incorrect. Increasing the timeout does not solve the unavailability of the bank that lasts longer than 15 minutes, and keep one Lambda in execution waiting for the available bank is inefficient and expensive. EventBridge has its own retry mechanism — the Lambda must fail quickly when the bank is unavailable, leaving the EventBridge/SQS manage retry.

Incorrect. SNS it also has withdrawals for its subscribers, but only for a limited period (does not persist indefinitely). Lambda by SNS just add a layer — SNS I would then have to invoke the Lambda Anyway. The correct solution for persistence of failed events is DLQ (SQS) + explicit retry, or EventBridge Archive/Replay.

Incorrect. Lambda Power Tuning optimizes memory size for better performance/cost, but does not resolve external bank unavailability — if the bank is out, more CPU The problem is of retry and persistence of events, not function performance..

questions.text: A company uses a Network Load Balancer (NLB) to balance traffic TCP/UDP for instance EC2. The team wants to ensure that each customer is always directed to the same instance EC2 during a session (IP stickiness), without needing to manage session status in the application. NLB implements this?
options: VPC Security Groups with rules that force IPs from specific clients to IPs from specific instances — deterministic routing ensures that the same client always reaches the same instance
Sticky Sessions with cookies managed by ALB (AWSALB/AWSALBCORS) — o ALB injects a cookie into the answer that identifies the instance, and the customer presents the cookie in subsequent requests
Session affinity via Amazon ElastiCache — the application stores session mapping in ElastiCache, and the NLB check the cache before each routing to direct to the correct instance

Sticky Sessions with IP-based stickiness of origin in NLB (Source IP affinity) — o NLB maintains a source IP mapping for the destination instance, ensuring that connections from the same source IP are always routed to the same instance
questions.explanation: Correct. NLB Supports Sticky Sessions based on source IP (Source IP affinity), not on cookies like ALB. When enabled, the NLB map the IP of origin (and optionally the port) to a specific instance, ensuring that connections from the same client are always sent to the same target during the configured stickiness period.
questions.hint: The NLB operates in Layer 4 (TCP/UDP) and has no cookies like the ALB — which stickiness mechanism uses, based on which connection attribute?
optionRationales: Correct. NLB Supports Sticky Sessions based on source IP (Source IP affinity), not on cookies like ALB. When enabled, the NLB map the IP of origin (and optionally the port) to a specific instance, ensuring that connections from the same client are always sent to the same target during the configured stickiness period.

Incorrect. Stickiness cookies (AWSALB) are a functionality of APPLICATION Load Balancer (ALB, Layer 7), not of the Network Load Balancer (NLB, Layer 4). The NLB operates in Layer 4 (TCP/UDP) and does not handle cookies HTTP — its stickiness mechanism is based on source IP (Source IP affinity), not on cookies.

Incorrect. NLB does not consult external services (such as ElastiCache) for routing decisions — it is a load balancing service on Layer 4 with own router logic. In addition, the statement specified 'without needing to manage state in the application', and using ElastiCache requires the application to manage the session.
Incorrect. Security Groups are firewalls that control which ports and IPs have access permission — do not route traffic to specific instances. Load Balancer (NLB/ALB), Not by Security Groups.

questions.text: A company uses AWS CloudFormation with StackSets to implement a configuration policy of CloudTrail in all 50 accounts of AWS Organization. When updating the StackSet template, the team wants the change to be automatically applied to all accounts without manually creating/deleteing StackSet instances. What functionality of StackSet supports this?
options: Create a Lambda with SDK of AWS that it will go through all the 50 accounts and execution `aws cloudformation update-stack` in each — this propagates the change without needing additional configuration in the StackSet
Enable Parameter Store Override in StackSet so that each account applies its own parameters when the template is centrally updated
Use AWS Config Conformance Packs with Auto-Remediation — Conformance Pack automatically detects and applies the desired configuration to all accounts without StackSets needing

CloudFormation StackSets with Auto Deployment enabled to Organizations — when enabled, StackSet automatically creates stack instances in new accounts added to the OR, removes deleted accounts, and can be configured to propagate template updates automatically to all existing accounts
questions.explanation: The StackSets with Auto Deployment for AWS Organizations automatically manages the stack instance life cycle: creates new accounts, removes accounts that exit the OR, and supports 'Automatic deployments' to keep instances up to date. By updating the StackSet template, changes can be spread to all OR accounts in an orchestrated way with competition control and tolerance to configurable failures.
questions.hint: What is the functionality of StackSet when integrated with AWS Organizations, automatically manages the creation and removal of stack instances as accounts enter and exit the OOs?
optionRationales: The StackSets with Auto Deployment for AWS Organizations automatically manages the stack instance life cycle: creates new accounts, removes accounts that exit the OR, and supports 'Automatic deployments' to keep instances up to date. By updating the StackSet template, changes can be spread to all OR accounts in an orchestrated way with competition control and tolerance to configurable failures.

Incorrect as a substitute. AWS Config Conformance Packs evaluate resource configuration compliance and may have automatic remediation — but they are not an infrastructure deployment mechanism like CloudFormation. To implement and manage features (such as configurations of CloudTrail) in a consistent manner in multiple accounts, CloudFormation StackSets is the right mechanism.

Incorrect as recommended approach. Lambda to iterate and update stacks individually is exactly what the StackSet with Auto Deployment eliminates. In addition to being more laborious, the Lambda would need cross-account permissions on all 50 accounts, error processing, coordinated rollback — everything StackSet already manages.

Incorrect. Override of parameters in StackSets allows individual instances to have parameter values different from the StackSet default, but is not an automatic template update propagation mechanism. Updating StackSet instances when the template changes is managed by Auto Deployment and by the UpdateStackSet operation'.

questions.text: A company has a microservices architecture with several functions Lambda which communicate via SQS. The team observed that when a function Lambda the downstream gets overloaded, the messages accumulate in the queue SQS, and when it recovers, try to process everything at once, causing new overloads in cascade. As the team can limit the rate of message processing in a row SQS by a function Lambda?
options: Configure the 'Competition' reserved in the function Lambda — by limiting the maximum number of parallel executions of Lambda, the maximum thread reading throughput SQS is implicitly limited, as more messages cannot be processed when all competing instances are occupied

Configure Maximum Competition in Event Source Mapping SQS for Lambda — a specific parameter that directly limits the number of parallel processes of that integration SQS→Lambda without affecting competition from other functions
Configure Event Source Mapping 'Batch Size' from Lambda for 1 (a message by invocation) — this forces sequential processing and effectively limits the throughput
Configure the line's Visibility Timeout SQS for a high value (ex.: 12 hours) — messages in processing are invisible for longer, limiting the rate of new messages available for processing
questions.explanation: Correct. Reserved Competition at Lambda sets the maximum number of parallel instances that can be executed. As the Event Source Mapping SQS invokes Lambda in parallel based on the available messages, limiting the reserved competition effectively limits the processing rate — protecting downstream systems and avoiding cascade overloads.
questions.hint: How you limit the number of parallel instances of a function Lambda which can be executed simultaneously, indirectly controlling the reading rate of the row SQS?
optionRationales: Correct. Reserved Competition at Lambda sets the maximum number of parallel instances that can be executed. As the Event Source Mapping SQS invokes Lambda in parallel based on the available messages, limiting the reserved competition effectively limits the processing rate — protecting downstream systems and avoiding cascade overloads.

Incorrect as a complete solution. Batch size 1 reduces the number of invocation messages but does not limit the number of parallel invocations — the Lambda it can still be invoked hundreds of times in parallel (one per message), generating similar overload. Reserved competition is effective throughput control.

Incorrect. Visibility Timeout High does not limit processing throughput — it only delays reprocessing of messages that are being processed. In practice, new messages that reach the queue are still visible immediately for processing, and the Lambda can still be invoked in high competition to prosecute them.

Partially correct but confused with the right answer. The 'Maximum Competition' in Event Source Mapping is a more recent feature (2023) which works in a similar way — but for the SAA-C03, the canonical response on throughput limitation SQS→Lambda is via Reserved Competition. Both serve similar purposes, but Reserved Competition is broader and is not Event Source Mapping specific.

questions.text: A company has a high-traffic web application hosted behind a ALB with Auto Scaling. The operations team realized that some instances EC2 are overloaded while others are idle, even with the ALB The team suspects that the ALB is disproportionately routed to some instances. ALB Target Group can solve this imbalance?
options: Configure Cross-Zone Load Balancing no ALB — this ensures that the ALB distributes traffic evenly between instances in all AZs, eliminating imbalances by AZ
Configure Stickiness in Target Group with TTL of 1 2nd — with TTL very short, the sessions are redistributed frequently, resulting in more even balance over time
Increase the number of instances EC2 no Auto Scaling Group — more instances distribute the burden, reducing the burden by instance and perceived imbalance

Enable Left Outstanding Requests (LOR) algorithm in Target Group — or ALB route each new request to the instance with the least number of requests in processing at that time, instead of the Round Robin standard that also distributes without considering the current load of each instance
questions.explanation: Right. ALB it is Round Robin, which distributes requests equally in sequence without considering the current load of each instance. If some requests take much longer (e.g. heavy wants), the instance accumulates more load. (LOR) considers the backlog of each instance, sending new requests to those who are less busy — resulting in more effective balancing when response times vary.
questions.hint: Which alternative algorithm to Round Robin considers the current backlog of each instance (processing requirements) when deciding where to send the next request?
optionRationales: Right. ALB it is Round Robin, which distributes requests equally in sequence without considering the current load of each instance. If some requests take much longer (e.g. heavy wants), the instance accumulates more load. (LOR) considers the backlog of each instance, sending new requests to those who are less busy — resulting in more effective balancing when response times vary.

Incorrect. Stickiness with TTL short would redistribute users frequently, but it could still cause imbalance if some users have heavier demands than others. Furthermore, Stickiness was designed to keep a user in the same instance (useful for local sessions), not for load balancing — its use to 'improve' the balancing is an anti-standard.

Incorrect for the specific problem. Adding more instances can help if the problem is of insufficient total capacity, but does not solve the algorithmic imbalance of Round Robin — with more instances, Round Robin can still overload some while others become idle if response times vary.

Partially relevant: Cross-Zone Load Balancing (which is already enabled by default in ALB) ensures that each node of the ALB distributes to instances in all AZs — solves imbalances by AZ. But the statement describes overload/ocociosity within instances (not by AZ), suggesting that the problem is the Round Robin router algorithm, not the cross-AZ distribution.

questions.text: A company uses Amazon S3 to store daily backups from your on-premises databases. Bucket has enabled versioning. A backup script accidentally overwritten a critical file with invalid data. As the team can recover the previous version of the file in S3?
options: List the versions of the object in S3 using ListObjectVersions, identify the previous version (by VersionId and LastModified), and copy that version back to the object (CopyObject with VersionId as source) or use the Console S3 to restore the previous version
Delete the current object in S3 — This creates a Marker Delete, doing the S3 automatically reveal the previous version as the current version of the object
Use S3 Replication to recover the previous version of a replicated destination pocket — replication keeps all versions in the destination for recovery cases
Restore the latest backup from before the incident stored in S3 Glacier — the life cycle of the bucket will automatically move older versions to the Glacier
questions.explanation: Right. S3 Versioning enabled, all versions of an object are retained. To recover the previous version: (1) list versions with ListObjectVersions to identify the correct version by VersionId and timestamp, (2) copy the old version over the current (CopyObject) or make GetObject by specifying VersionId. The console S3 has a graphical interface for this.
questions.hint: With S3 Enabled versioning, all versions are retained. As you identify and access an earlier specific version of an object — which parameter uniquely identifies a version?
optionRationales: Right. S3 Versioning enabled, all versions of an object are retained. To recover the previous version: (1) list versions with ListObjectVersions to identify the correct version by VersionId and timestamp, (2) copy the old version over the current (CopyObject) or make GetObject by specifying VersionId. The console S3 has a graphical interface for this.

Incorrect. The question specifies that the versioning is enabled and the file was overwritten (new version created). The previous version is still in S3 Standard (unless a lifecycle rule has moved it to Glacier — the statement does not mention this). S3 no need to restore the Glacier.

Incorrect as a direct solution for the case described. The statement does not mention a configured replication loop. In addition, with enabled versioning, the previous version of the file is already available in MESMO Bucket — no replicated Bucket is required to recover it.

Incorrect. A 'delete' in a versioned pocket creates a Marker Delete (does not delete the object) — subsequent GETs return a 404, not the previous version. To reveal the previous version, it would be necessary to delete the Delete Marker, not the object. Furthermore, 'delete the current object' (the version with invalid data) without specifying the VersionId would only create a Delete Marker, would not reveal the good version.

questions.text: A company uses Amazon ECS with Fargate during an application. During a deployment, the team wants to ensure that the old version of the tasks continue to serve traffic until the new tasks are completely healthy and the ALB has confirmed the health checks. What configuration in ECS Service controls this safe deployment behavior?
options: Use ECS Rolling Update with constraints task placement that require new and old tasks never to coexist in the same instance (distinctTribunal) — the ECS waits for the old instance to finish before launching the new

Configure Deployment Configuration with 'Minimum Healthy Percent' and 'Maximum Percent' no ECS Service — minimum healthy percentage ensures that a minimum percentage of old tasks continue to run during deployment, and maximum percentage controls the total (old + new) tasks allowed, preventing the new version from replacing old tasks before being healthy
Use AWS CodeDeploy with typical deployment 'ECS Blue/Green' — or CodeDeploy manage the safe replacement of tasks, ensuring that the ALB only direct traffic to new tasks after health check confirmed
Configure a ECS Service Discovery with Route 53 — the Discovery Service records the new tasks in DNS and the Route 53 health check removes old ones automatically when new ones are healthy
questions.explanation: Correct. Deployment Configuration no ECS Service has two parameters: 'Minimum Healthy Percent' (ex.: 100%) ensures that 100% of the tasks of the desired count continue healthy during deployment — ECS only remove old tasks when the new ones pass in the health check of ALB. 'Maximum Percentage (ex.: 200%) allows you to launch new tasks (add above the desired) before removing the old ones. Together, ensure zero-downtime and secure replacement.
questions.hint: Which parameter of 'Deployment Configuration' no ECS Service ensures that a minimum percentage of old tasks continue running until new ones pass the health checks of ALB?
optionRationales: Correct. Deployment Configuration no ECS Service has two parameters: 'Minimum Healthy Percent' (ex.: 100%) ensures that 100% of the tasks of the desired count continue healthy during deployment — ECS only remove old tasks when the new ones pass in the health check of ALB. 'Maximum Percentage (ex.: 200%) allows you to launch new tasks (add above the desired) before removing the old ones. Together, ensure zero-downtime and secure replacement.

Incorrect to Fargate. Task Placement Constraints (as a separate Forum) apply to clusters EC2, no Fargate (which does not explicitly manage instances). Furthermore, forcing old and new ones never coexist would cause downtime during the transition. Deployment Configuration (min/max percent) is the correct and applicable mechanism to Fargate.

Incorrect for the scenario with ALB. Service Discovery with Route 53 is suitable for service-to-service communication (internal microservices), not for the safe deployment scenario with ALB. When the ECS Service uses ALB, the safe deployment mechanism is the Deployment Configuration (min/max healthy percent) combined with the health checks of the ALB.

Correct conceptually but not the configuration NATIVA of the ECS Service that the statement asks. CodeDeploy ECS Blue/Green is a valid and powerful option for deployment, but requires integration with CodeDeploy separate. Deployment Configuration (min/max percent) is the native configuration of ECS Service that controls this behavior directly.

questions.text: A company has a cluster Amazon EMR for data processing with Spark. The cluster has a Master Node and multiple Core Nodes. The team wants to ensure resilience to Core Nodes failures without data loss in processing. HDFS of the EMR protects against Core Nodes failure?
options: The HDFS no EMR uses replication of data blocks between multiple Core Nodes (replication factor) 3 by default) — if a Core Node fails, the HDFS automatically re-replicates lost blocks to other available Core Nodes without data loss
The EMR makes automatic backup of data from HDFS for the S3 each 5 minutes — if a Core Node fails, the data is restored from S3 automatically for the remaining nodes
Master Node keeps copies of all data processed by Core Nodes — if a Core Node fails, Master Node redistributes its data to the remaining Core Nodes
The EMR use Auto Scaling to automatically replace failed Core Nodes with new instances — lost data from the old node is re-processed by Spark using Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) Recovery
questions.explanation: Correct. HDFS (Hadoop Distributed File System) EMR uses the configured replication factor (standard) 3) to store copies of each data block in multiple Core Nodes. If a Core Node fails, the HDFS detects sub-replicated blocks and automatically creates copies in the available nodes, maintaining data integrity.
questions.hint: The HDFS no EMR uses a data redundancy mechanism between multiple DataNodes (Core Nodes) — what is this mechanism, and what is the standard redundancy factor?
optionRationales: Correct. HDFS (Hadoop Distributed File System) EMR uses the configured replication factor (standard) 3) to store copies of each data block in multiple Core Nodes. If a Core Node fails, the HDFS detects sub-replicated blocks and automatically creates copies in the available nodes, maintaining data integrity.

Incorrect. EMR does not backup automatically periodically from HDFS for S3 (this would need to be explicitly configured via DistCp or EMRFS). The resilience of the HDFS comes from the REPLECTION of blocks between Core Nodes, not backup to S3. S3 is used as external storage (via EMRFS) when the data needs to persist beyond the cluster life cycle.

Partially correct about Auto Scaling to be able to replace us, but the data protection mechanism is not DAG Spark recovery (which is for tolerance to computer task failures, not protection of stored data). HDFS is the mechanism that protects data stored in Core Nodes against loss due to node failure.

Incorrect. Master Node manages the metadata of HDFS (NameNode) and coordinates the cluster, but DO NOT store copies of CoreNodes block data. Block data is exclusively in CoreNodes (DataNodes no HDFS). Master Node knows ONDE the blocks are (namespace), and after a failure, directs the replication to other available Core Nodes.

questions.text: A company uses Amazon SQS with a Lambda the team realized that in periods of high traffic, the Lambda failure with competition limit errors (throttling). Unprocessed messages expire in the queue and are lost before the Lambda What combination of configurations solves the problem of message loss without increasing the competition of Lambda?
options: Increase Batch Size in Event Source Mapping to 10.000 messages — a Lambda will process more invocation messages, reducing the number of invocations needed and throttling

Enable Long Polling in the queue SQS (waitTimeSeconds=20) — the long polling reduces empty chick calls and increases processing efficiency, allowing the Lambda processes more messages with the same competition
Migration to a queue SQS FIFO — rows FIFO process messages in order and guarantee exactly-once delivery, eliminating duplicate messages that cause excessive throttling

Increase Message Retention Period from the queue SQS (maximum 14 days) and set up a DLQ for messages that exceed maxReceiveCount — the long period retention ensures that messages do not expire while waiting for processing, and the DLQ capture messages that failed repeatedly for further analysis
questions.explanation: Correct. Message Retention Longer period (up to 14 days) ensures that messages do not expire while the Lambda is being throtted and the backlog exists. DLQ It takes messages that have exceeded the maximum number of attempts — ensuring that they are not silently discarded. Together, these two mechanisms ensure that no messages are lost, even without increasing competition from the Lambda.
questions.hint: To ensure that messages are not PERDIDAS while awaiting processing with throttling, which row parameter SQS how long do you control messages? And what mechanism captures messages that have exhausted attempts?
optionRationales: Correct. Message Retention Longer period (up to 14 days) ensures that messages do not expire while the Lambda is being throtted and the backlog exists. DLQ It takes messages that have exceeded the maximum number of attempts — ensuring that they are not silently discarded. Together, these two mechanisms ensure that no messages are lost, even without increasing competition from the Lambda.

Incorrect as a solution for message expiration. Long Polling reduces cost (less empty chicks) and message detection latency, but does not solve the problem of messages expiring when competition from Lambda is exhausted — bottleneck is the processing capacity of Lambda, not the polling frequency.

Incorrect. Increasing the Batch Size reduces the number of calls but does not necessarily reduce the throttling — if maximum competition has been reached, new calls are blocked independently of the batch size. Moreover, very large batch sizes increase the latency and the risk of timeout of the Lambda by summons.

Incorrect. SQS FIFO does not resolve throttling of Lambda — throttling is caused by the limit of competition of the Lambda, Not for duplicate messages. FIFO have throughput MENOR (300 TPS without batching vs. almost unlimited in the Standard), which would make the backlog problem worse.
