questions.text: A company uses Amazon CloudFront to distribute content of a ALB The engineering team wants you to CloudFront serve cached content based on the path of URL: objects in /api/* should never be cached (TTL=0), as objects in /static/* should be cached by 24 hours. What functionality of CloudFront allows this differentiated configuration by way?
options: Cache Behaviors no CloudFront — each Behavior Cache maps a path pattern (ex.: /api/*, /static/*) to independent configurations of TTL, referred headers, and origin; the order of precedence of the behaviors (more specific first) determines which configuration is applied to each request
Use Lambda@Edge no viewer request to modify or TTL based on the path — the function inspects the path and defines the correct Cache-Control header before the check cache
Create two distributions CloudFront separate — one for /api/* with TTL=0 and another for /static/* with TTL=24h — and use Route 53 to route the correct paths for each distribution

Configure Origin Response Heads Separate policies for each path — the origin returns different Cache-Control headers for /api/* and /static/*, and CloudFront automatically respect these headers by the way
questions.explanation: That's right. CloudFront allow different configurations by path pattern. Default Cache Behavior applies to all path not covered by other behaviors. Specific Behaviors (such as /api/* and /static/*) are evaluated in order of precedence — more specific have priority. Each behavior has its own configurations of TTL, headers, cookies, and origin independently.
questions.hint: What is the functionality of CloudFront map road patterns from URL to independent cache settings within a single distribution?
optionRationales: That's right. CloudFront allow different configurations by path pattern. Default Cache Behavior applies to all path not covered by other behaviors. Specific Behaviors (such as /api/* and /static/*) are evaluated in order of precedence — more specific have priority. Each behavior has its own configurations of TTL, headers, cookies, and origin independently.

Partially correct: or CloudFront respects Cache-Control headers of origin, but this would be configured in ORIGEM (ALB/application), not in CloudFront. In addition, without separate Behaviors Cache, the CloudFront I wouldn't know that /api/* and /static/* must have different behaviors — would apply the same cache policy to both. Cache Behaviors are the correct feature for this differentiation in the CloudFront.

Incorrect and unnecessarily complex. Creating two distributions for the same domain is not possible simply (each distribution has its own domain CloudFront) and it would require logic of custom routing. Cache Behaviors within a single distribution are designed exactly for this case of differentiation by way.

Incorrect as a primary approach. Lambda@Edge can dynamically modify behaviors, but for a static rule of TTL by way (something that never changes), using Cache Behaviors is much simpler, more efficient and without running cost by invoking Lambda. Lambda@Edge is suitable for dynamic logic that cannot be expressed in static settings.

questions.text: A company uses Application Load Balancer (ALB) for a web application. API return large binary files (PDFs, images). The team perceives high latency in these endpoints and wants to migrate to a balancer that supports TCP passthrough without termination SSL, to reduce overhead processing. Load Balancer AWS meets this requirement?
options: Classic Load Balancer in mode TCP — o CLB supports TCP passthrough when configured in protocol mode TCP, no termination SSL
Application Load Balancer with IP type target groups — IP type targets support IP type bypasses SSL and direct connections directly to the endpoints without termination SSL no ALB
Gateway Load Balancer (GWLB) — operates in Layer 3 and forwards IP packages directly to network applications without any inspection or termination SSL

Network Load Balancer (NLB) operating in Layer 4 (TCP/UDP) — o NLB makes passthrough connections TCP without inspecting the content HTTP, allowing SSL is terminated directly by the instances EC2 backend, reducing overhead processing in the balancer
questions.explanation: Correct. NLB operates in Layer 4 (TCP/UDP) and can do TCP passthrough — the connection TLS is passed directly to the backend without the NLB finish/inspect or SSL. This reduces the processing overhead SSL no load balancer (which is processed by backend instances) and is suitable for applications that need low latency for binary transfers.
questions.hint: Which AWS Load Balancer operates in Layer 4 (TCP/UDP) and can passthrough connections without finishing SSL, delegating processing SSL for backend servers?
optionRationales: Correct. NLB operates in Layer 4 (TCP/UDP) and can do TCP passthrough — the connection TLS is passed directly to the backend without the NLB finish/inspect or SSL. This reduces the processing overhead SSL no load balancer (which is processed by backend instances) and is suitable for applications that need low latency for binary transfers.

Incorrect. ALB SEMPRE Finished SSL — independent of the target group type (institution, IP), Lambda). The ALB It's a Layer 7 load balancer inspecting the content HTTP to make decisions about routing. TCP passthrough without termination SSL no load balancer, o NLB is necessary.

Partially Historically Correct: The Classic Load Balancer supported mode TCP no termination SSL. However, CLB is in maintenance mode and its replacement is the NLB for Layer cases 4. The NLB is the correct and recommended response by AWS for new deployments.

Incorrect for this use case. The Gateway Load Balancer is designed to insert virtual network applications (firewalls), IDS/IPS) on the road of traffic of a VPC using the protocol GENEVE. Not an application load balancer — your usage case is network app traffic inspection, not web application load balancer.

questions.text: A company uses Amazon ElastiCache for Redis for caching user sessions. With application growth, Redis is reaching the memory limit of a single node, causing data avoidance. The team wants to scale the memory capacity of Redis without downtime. Which ElastiCache configuration allows to increase the total memory capacity of Redis beyond the limits of a single node?
options: ElastiCache Redis without Cluster Mode with multiple Read Replicas — read replicas increase the total memory capacity of the cluster, as each replica stores additional data
Configure the Tiered Cashing Redis with Amazon S3 as secondary ter — data that do not fit in the memory of Redis are automatically moved to S3, effectively increasing total capacity

ElastiCache Redis with Enabled Cluster Mode — automatically distributes data between multiple shards using hash slots, increasing the total memory capacity proportional to the number of configured shards, with each shard being able to have replicas for reading and availability
Perform vertical scaling (institution type upgrade) for a more memory instance — ElastiCache allows you to modify the instance type without downtime using the 'Modify Cluster' mechanism'
questions.explanation: Correct. Redis Cluster Mode distributes data between multiple shards (automatic partitioning via hash slots). Each shard has a primary and optional replicas. The total memory capacity is the sum of all primarys — allowing horizontal scaling beyond the limits of a single node. With Cluster Mode enabled, it is possible to add online shards with redistribution slots.
questions.hint: Which ElastiCache Redis mode distributes data between multiple shards (horizontal partitioning) to increase total memory capacity beyond the limits of a single node?
optionRationales: Correct. Redis Cluster Mode distributes data between multiple shards (automatic partitioning via hash slots). Each shard has a primary and optional replicas. The total memory capacity is the sum of all primarys — allowing horizontal scaling beyond the limits of a single node. With Cluster Mode enabled, it is possible to add online shards with redistribution slots.

Incorrect. Read Replicas in Redis without Cluster Mode are COPY COMPLETAS of primary data — they increase the ability of LEITURA (throughput), not total memory. Each replica contains the MESMOS data that the primary, then the total memory capacity does not increase with more replicas. To increase the memory capacity, partitioning via Cluster Mode is necessary.

Partially correct: vertical scaling is possible but has limitations (maximum instance type available) and usually causes a brief interruption during modification. Furthermore, it does not scale indefinitely — eventually the major instance type will also be insufficient. Cluster Mode with multiple shards is the solution to scale beyond the limits of a single node without these trade-offs.

Incorrect. There is no native resource of 'Tiered Caching with S3' in ElastiCache for Redis. Redis is a cache in memory — has no ability to tie to S3 Automatically. Cluster Mode is the right solution to increase memory capacity.

questions.text: A company has a serverless application using API Gateway + Lambda processing requests that sometimes take 25 seconds to complete. Users are receiving timeout errors. API Gateway has a timeout configured from 29 What is the most likely cause and the solution?
options: The Amazon API Gateway has a maximum timeout HARD LIMIT of 29 seconds for integration synchronous calls — for requests that take more than 29 seconds, it is necessary to migrate to an asynchronous architecture: API Gateway immediately returns one 202 Accepted, Lambda process in background, and the customer polling or receives notification by WebSocket/SNS
The problem is the default timeout of the function Lambda (3 (seconds) — increase the timeout of Lambda for 30 seconds will resolve the timeout error in API Gateway

Use Lambda Provided Competition to eliminate cold startups — the 25 seconds are caused by cold start of Lambda, and provided competition ensures that warm instances are available to respond in milliseconds
Migration from API Gateway REST for API Gateway HTTP API — HTTP APIs have a timeout of 60 seconds, sufficient for operations of 25 seconds
questions.explanation: Correct. API Gateway has an absolute maximum timeout of 29 seconds for synchronous integrations — not configurable above that. For operations that exceed this limit, the solution is asynchronous architecture: the client makes the call and receives a request ID (202 Accepted), a Lambda process anointingly, and the customer receives the result via polling (GET /status/{id}), WebSocket (API Gateway WebSocket API), or push notification (SNS/SES).
questions.hint: The API Gateway has an absolute maximum limit of how long an integration response can wait. What is that limit, and what architecture resolves requests that exceed that limit?
optionRationales: Correct. API Gateway has an absolute maximum timeout of 29 seconds for synchronous integrations — not configurable above that. For operations that exceed this limit, the solution is asynchronous architecture: the client makes the call and receives a request ID (202 Accepted), a Lambda process anointingly, and the customer receives the result via polling (GET /status/{id}), WebSocket (API Gateway WebSocket API), or push notification (SNS/SES).

Incorrect over the limit. The standard timeout of Lambda It's 3 seconds but it's CONFIGURABLE until 15 However, even with Lambda configured for 30 minutes of timeout, or API Gateway has its own hard limit of 29 seconds. Lambda take more than 29 seconds, the API Gateway will return timeout to the client independent of timeout from Lambda.

Incorrect. Cold beginnings of Lambda last milliseconds a few seconds at most — no 25 The statement describes the processing that genuinely takes 25 (not a start-up delay). Provided Competition would not solve a long-term processing.

Incorrect. Both types of API Gateway (REST and HTTP API) have the same hard limit of 29 seconds for integration with Lambda syncrona. Migration between types does not increase timeout beyond 29 seconds.

questions.text: A company uses Amazon S3 to store analytics data. The data has an unpredictable access pattern — some objects are accessed frequently for weeks, then they are almost out of access for months, and occasionally they are accessed again. The team wants to minimize storage costs without needing to manage class transitions manually or incur retriival rates. S3 is more suitable?
options: S3 Standard-IA (Infrequent Access) with lifecycle rules for transition after 30 days — data that are not accessible by 30 days are moved to Standard-IA automatically, reducing storage costs
S3 Standard with lifecycle rules that move objects to S3 Glacier after 90 days without access — Glacier offers the lowest long-term storage cost
S3 One Zone-IA — stores data in only one AZ at lower cost than Standard-IA, suitable for data that may be reproducible in case of AZ loss and have infrequent access

S3 Intelligent-Tiering — automatically monitors the access patterns of each object and moves between third parties (Frequent Access, Infrequent Access, Archive Instant Access) without retrieving fees and no penalty for early removal, ideal for unpredictable access patterns
questions.explanation: Correct.. S3 Intelligent-Tiering uses ML to monitor the access pattern of each object and automatically moves between third parties based on the actual access frequency — without manual intervention. It does not charge retrieval fees for frequent, infrequent and instantaneous access third parties. There is a small rate of monitoring per object, but for objects larger than 128KB, cost is usually compensated by storage savings.
questions.hint: Which class S3 Automatically monitor access patterns without manual intervention, without retrieving fees, and without removal penalties — designed for unpredictable access?
optionRationales: Correct.. S3 Intelligent-Tiering uses ML to monitor the access pattern of each object and automatically moves between third parties based on the actual access frequency — without manual intervention. It does not charge retrieval fees for frequent, infrequent and instantaneous access third parties. There is a small rate of monitoring per object, but for objects larger than 128KB, cost is usually compensated by storage savings.

Incorrect for IMPRESSIBLE standards. Standard-IA has a retriival rate per GB and a minimum penalty of removal of 30 days — objects accessed earlier will pay for 30 For unpredictable patterns where objects can be accessed again frequently, Standard-IA retrieval rates make the cost unpredictable. Intelligent-Tiering has no retrieval rates.

Incorrect because Glacier has significant retriival rates and latency (minutes to hours) to recover objects. The statement describes objects that are 'occasionally accessed again' — Glacier would be inadequate because access to objects on the Glacier incurs recovery and delay costs, conflicting with the requirement of 'no retriival rates''.

Incorrect due to lack of adequate durability and the same limitations of the Standard-IA. S3 One Zone-IA has less durability (99.5% vs 99.999999999% of the S3 Standard) and has retriival rates per GB. For analytics data with unpredictable pattern, One Zone-IA presents a risk of data loss (if AZ fails) and is not suitable for unpredictable access patterns with occasional access.

questions.text: A company uses Amazon DynamoDB for a global e-commerce application with strong consistent readouts. The team observed that some partitions are receiving much more traffic than others ('hot partitions'), causing throttling errors. Data is accessed by ProductID as a key partition, and the most popular products cause hot partitions. What technique solves the hot partitions problem without changing the data model completely?
options: Enable DynamoDB Adaptive Capacity — Automatically distributes throughput from the least used to the most used partitions, eliminating throttling in hot partitions without key change
Migratory to DynamoDB Global Tables — multi-region replication distributes readings across regions, reducing the load on each individual partition in the primary region

Write Shadding — add a random suffix to the partition key (e.g. ProductID)_1, ProductID_2, ProductID_N) distributes a popular product between N shards/partitions; readings need to consult all N shards and combine results in application

DynamoDB Auto Scaling — enable Auto Scaling in the tables with hot partitions makes the DynamoDB automatically distributes hot partitions between multiple physical partitions without the need for key change
questions.explanation: Write Sharing artificially distributes a hot item between multiple partitions adding a suffix (1 a N) to the partition key. The load is distributed by up to N different partitions, each receiving 1/N of the original traffic. In reading, the application consults all N shards (ProductID_1 a ProductID_N) and combines the results. It is the standard technique to solve hot partitions in DynamoDB.
questions.hint: What key design technique does it have? DynamoDB artificially distributes a 'hot' item between multiple partitions by adding a variable component to the partition key?
optionRationales: Write Sharing artificially distributes a hot item between multiple partitions adding a suffix (1 a N) to the partition key. The load is distributed by up to N different partitions, each receiving 1/N of the original traffic. In reading, the application consults all N shards (ProductID_1 a ProductID_N) and combines the results. It is the standard technique to solve hot partitions in DynamoDB.

Wrong about the mechanism. DynamoDB Auto Scaling automatically adjusts the provided throughput (RUS/WCUs) in response to demand — does not distribute data between partitions automatically. Hot partitions caused by unbalanced access to keys persist even with Auto Scaling, because the Auto Scaling increases total capacity but not balancing between individual partitions.

Partially correct: or DynamoDB Adaptive Capacity (Already enabled by default since 2019) redistribute throughput between partitions dynamically. However, it has limit: the adaptive capacity helps for temporary bursts but does not solve persistent hot partitions where a partition SEMPRE receives more traffic than your share — in this case, Write Shadding is needed to distribute the load structurally.

Incorrect for this specific problem. Global Tables replicates data in multiple regions for low latency global access, but does not solve hot partitions within a single region. Users from the same region will still access the same partitions of the local replica, causing the same hot partition problem..

questions.text: A company is migrating a monolithic application for microservices using containers. Containers need shared access to a file system for reading/writing temporary files during processing, with low latency. Containers run on Amazon ECS with Fargate. Which shared storage solution meets this requirement?
options: Amazon EBS Multi-Attach — a volume EBS with Multi-Attach enabled can be mounted in multiple tasks ECS Fargate simultaneously for shared access with very low latency
Amazon S3 with AWS SDK built into containers — containers make GetObject/PutObject for S3 to read/write temporary files, and S3 guarantees consistency of reading after writing
Amazon FSx for Lustre — High Performance File System for HPC with sub-millisecond latency, integrated with ECS Fargate for shared processing workloads

Amazon EFS (Elastic File System) mounted in the tasks ECS Fargate — o EFS is a file system NFS managed that can be mounted in multiple containers simultaneously (ReadWriteMany), with native support in ECS Fargate by volume definitions
questions.explanation: Correct. EFS supports ReadWriteMany access (multiple containers in multiple hosts simultaneously), is fully managed, and has native integration with the ECS Fargate (configured in the Task Definitions as a type volume EFS). Latency is tens of milliseconds, suitable for most cases of shared access.
questions.hint: What storage service does the AWS is a file system NFS managed that supports simultaneous assembly in multiple containers ECS Fargate (ReadWriteMany)?
optionRationales: Correct. EFS supports ReadWriteMany access (multiple containers in multiple hosts simultaneously), is fully managed, and has native integration with the ECS Fargate (configured in the Task Definitions as a type volume EFS). Latency is tens of milliseconds, suitable for most cases of shared access.

Incorrect for two reasons: (1) EBS Multi-Attach supports maximum 16 cases EC2 SIMULTANEAMENTE — and the ECS FARGATE does not support volumes EBS (o Fargate does not manage instances EC2 explicitly). EBS is for volume of instances EC2; EFS is the shared storage solution for containers Fargate. (2) EBS Multi-Attach requires application-level lock management (file system cluster-aware)).

Incorrect to use 'file system''. S3 is an object store — is not a file system with mount point semantics. Application temporary files that require file system access (open, write, read, seek, close) do not work natively with the API of the S3. In addition, S3 has a higher latency (~100ms) for small operations compared to EFS for frequent access to temporary files.

Incorrect for this use case. FSx for Lustre is a high performance file system for loads HPC (Machine Learning, Big Data, CFD) — does not support task mounting ECS Fargate native (is designed for EC2). In addition, it would be oversized and much more expensive for temporary container files.

questions.text: A company uses Amazon API Gateway REST API with integration Lambda for a high demand service. The team observed that many requests receive the same answer (data from products that change only once an hour). API Gateway can be enabled to reduce invocations of Lambda and decrease the latency of the responses?
options: API Gateway Usage Plans with Throttling by API Key — limiting the number of requests per second per user reduces the load on Lambda by decreasing the total volume of calls
Lambda@Edge integrated with API Gateway — the Lambda@Edge processes the most user-friendly requests in the network CloudFront, eliminating network latency up to the API Gateway in the region

API Gateway Caching — enable cache in the stage of API Gateway stores integration responses by one TTL configured (1 second 1 time); subsequent identical requests are answered directly from the cache of API Gateway, without invoking Lambda
CloudFront in front of the API Gateway with TTL of 1 time — o CloudFront caches the answers of the API and serves as the edge location closer to the user, reducing both latency and invocations Lambda
questions.explanation: Correct. API Gateway has a native response cache (in stage) that stores the responses by TTL configurable. Requirements that match in key cache (URL path, query strings, configured headers) receive the cache response, reducing invocations Lambda and latency. The cache is by stage (e.g. production) and has cost per hour based on the configured size (0.5 GB a 237 GB).
questions.hint: The API Gateway has a native response cache that can be enabled by stage — what is the name of that feature?
optionRationales: Correct. API Gateway has a native response cache (in stage) that stores the responses by TTL configurable. Requirements that match in key cache (URL path, query strings, configured headers) receive the cache response, reducing invocations Lambda and latency. The cache is by stage (e.g. production) and has cost per hour based on the configured size (0.5 GB a 237 GB).

Partially correct: CloudFront + API Gateway is a valid standard for caching API. However, for a API REST with data from products that change per hour, the CloudFront cachey answers GET/HEAD by default but requires careful cache key configuration (including authentication headers) to avoid serving data from one user to another. API Gateway Caching is the most direct native solution for this case.

Incorrect. Lambda@Edge executes code in edge locations of the CloudFront, but this does not automatically create a cache — each request still invokes the Lambda@Edge and then the Lambda integration of the API Gateway. To cache answers and reduce invocations, an explicit cache would be required (CloudFront cache or API Cache Gateway).

Incorrect. Usage Plans with Throttling limit to QUANTIDADE of calls that a user can make, rejecting excesses with 429 Too Many Requests — does not hide answers. This would reduce traffic by rate limiting (blocking requests), not by serving cached answers in a transparent way.

questions.text: A company has a database Aurora PostgreSQL running a workload OLTP intensive with many simultaneous connections of multiple functions Lambda. The team is seeing 'too many connections' errors because Lambda creates a new connection by invocation. AWS solves the problem of managing connections between Lambda and Aurora without changing the query code SQL?
options: Amazon RDS Proxy — acts as a connecting pooling intermediary between functions Lambda and the Aurora; maintains a pool of pre-established connections with the bank and multiplexes the Lambdas connections by the pool, drastically reducing the number of real connections to the bank
Migration from Aurora PostgreSQL for Amazon DynamoDB — o DynamoDB has no connection limits and scale automatically with the number of requests Lambda
Use Aurora Serverless v2 instead of Aurora Provisioned — Aurora Serverless automatically scales the demand-based connection capacity, without 'too many connections' errors'
Increase max_connections no Aurora PostgreSQL via Parameter Group — Aurora supports tens of thousands of simultaneous connections, so increase the limit resolves 'too many connections'
questions.explanation: Correct. RDS Proxy maintains a pool of persistent connections to the database and allows multiple invocations Lambda share these connections. Even with hundreds of Lambdas invoked simultaneously, the RDS Proxy can serve all using a much smaller number of real connections to the bank Aurora. It is completely transparent for the query code SQL — only the connection endpoint changes.
questions.hint: What service AWS acts as a proxy for connecting pooling between Lambda and RDS/Aurora, reducing the number of simultaneous connections to the bank without changing the code SQL?
optionRationales: Correct. RDS Proxy maintains a pool of persistent connections to the database and allows multiple invocations Lambda share these connections. Even with hundreds of Lambdas invoked simultaneously, the RDS Proxy can serve all using a much smaller number of real connections to the bank Aurora. It is completely transparent for the query code SQL — only the connection endpoint changes.

Incorrect as scalable solution. Increasing max_connections requires more memory per connection — each PostgreSQL connection uses ~5-10 MB of memory on the server. With Lambda being able to create hundreds of simultaneous connections and growing with traffic, increase the limit only postpones the problem, besides degrading performance with many active connections. RDS Proxy is the right architectural solution.

Incorrect. Aurora Serverless v2 ACUs scale (Aurora Capacity Units) based on CPU and memory — but the problem of 'too many connections' persists even in Serverless, as each PostgreSQL connection still uses significant memory. Serverless can help with capacity scaling, but does not solve the fundamental problem of managing short-term connections of Lambda. RDS Proxy is needed for this case.

Incorrect. PostgreSQL migration relational to DynamoDB NoSQL is a huge architectural change that requires redesign of the data model and queries — is not a practical solution to the problem of connections. RDS Proxy solves the problem without database migration.

questions.text: A company uses Amazon CloudFront to distribute a web application protected by authentication. The team wants only authenticated users can download objects from the pocket S3 way CloudFront, without exposing the pocket S3 Publicly. How to set this up correctly with the CloudFront?
options: Use CloudFront Signed URLs generated by S3 — o S3 generates URLs with temporary signature that expire after a period, and the CloudFront validates the signature before serving the content

Configure the Bucket Policy S3 to allow only requests with the header 'X-CloudFront-Secret: <secret value>' — or CloudFront injects this custom header into all original requests, and the S3 block requests without the header
Enable S3 Block Public Access — this automatically restricts access to the pocket only via CloudFront, without the need for additional policies

Use Origin Access Control (OAC) no CloudFront — grants to CloudFront own identity to access the pocket S3 private, and the bucket policy only allows access to the OAC; unauthenticated users who try to access the S3 directly receive 403, and the CloudFront can be protected by Lambda@Edge or Cognito for user authentication
questions.explanation: Correct. O Origin Access Control (OAC) is the modern mechanism (substitute of OAI) to ensure that the CloudFront be the only customer who can access the pocket S3. The bucket policy allows access only to the CloudFront way OAC, and the pocket remains private. For user authentication, Lambda@Edge or CloudFront Signed URLs/Cookies with validation via Cognito are the recommended additional approaches.
questions.hint: What is the mechanism of CloudFront creates an identity that CloudFront uses to access pocketes S3 private — being the modern replacement of the old Origin Access Identity (OAI)?
optionRationales: Correct. O Origin Access Control (OAC) is the modern mechanism (substitute of OAI) to ensure that the CloudFront be the only customer who can access the pocket S3. The bucket policy allows access only to the CloudFront way OAC, and the pocket remains private. For user authentication, Lambda@Edge or CloudFront Signed URLs/Cookies with validation via Cognito are the recommended additional approaches.

Incorrect. S3 does not evaluate headers HTTP customised in the policies — the policies only assess conditions such as ARN of the main, IP of origin, and condition keys of the S3. Using a secret header is a technique used with CUSTOM ORIGINS (as ALB/EC2), not with S3 which requires OAC/OAI for direct access control.

Incorrect. S3 Block Public Access blocks settings that would make the bucket public (ACLs and bucket policies that grant public access) — but does not automatically create permission for CloudFront. No OAC/OAI and an explicit bucket policy, CloudFront I couldn't access the private bucket objects either..

Incorrect. Signed URLs are generated by CloudFront (not for S3) using a key pair of CloudFront. They control access to specific objects via CloudFront for a limited period — useful for distribution of temporary content. But the question asks access based on user authentication (not just temporary URLs), and the Bucket protection mechanism itself is the OAC, not signed URLs.

questions.text: A company uses Amazon Athena to analyze stored logs in S3 in format JSON. The cherries are taking a long time. (>10 minutes) and generating high cost (scanning many GB). The team wants to optimize performance and cost without changing the query tool. What change in format and organization of data has the greatest impact on performance and cost in Athena?
options: Convert data from JSON for columnar format Parquet or ORC And partition the data into S3 by date/hour (ex.: s3://Bucket/logs/year=2024/month=01/day=15/) — o Public Prosecutor's Office/ORC allows the Athena make column pruning (read only the necessary columns), and partitions allow the Athena make partition pruning (scan only files from filtered partitions)
Increase the number of DPUs (Data Processing Units) Athena to process more data in parallel, reducing the execution time of queries
Compress files JSON with GZIP before you store them S3 — compression reduces the bytes transferred from S3 for the Athena, decreasing both the time and the cost of the desires
Use Athena Query Result Reuse — the Athena reuses results of recent identical queries (up to 7 days), eliminating the need to scan data again for repeated queries
questions.explanation: Correct. The combination of column format + partitioning has the greatest impact on Athena: (1) Parquet/ORC allows you to read only the columns needed for the query (column pruning) — if the query uses 3 of 50 columns, or Athena read only ~6% data; (2) Partitioning allows filters WHERE in the partition column do the Athena do not scan non-relevant partitions. Together, they drastically reduce the scanned GB — which is what determines both the cost and the time of the query.
questions.hint: Which two storage features have the greatest impact on performance and cost of Athena — one related to the format (columns vs. lines) and another to the organization in S3?
optionRationales: Correct. The combination of column format + partitioning has the greatest impact on Athena: (1) Parquet/ORC allows you to read only the columns needed for the query (column pruning) — if the query uses 3 of 50 columns, or Athena read only ~6% data; (2) Partitioning allows filters WHERE in the partition column do the Athena do not scan non-relevant partitions. Together, they drastically reduce the scanned GB — which is what determines both the cost and the time of the query.

Incorrect as greater impact. Compression GZIP files JSON reduces the stored size and read bytes of S3, but the Athena still need to decompress and parsley TODOS the fields of TODOS records JSON even if the query uses only a few columns — there is no benefit of column pruning in JSON tablet., GZIP is not splittable (the entire file needs to be processed as a unit), limiting parallelism./ORC tablets are much higher.

Incorrect. Athena does not have a 'DPUs' configuration that the user adjusts directly (different from AWS Glue using DPUs). Athena automatically scale data-based processing. Partially correct: Query Result Reuse eliminates executions of recent IDENTICAL Queries, but does not improve the performance of queries NOVAS or different. questions.text: A company uses AWS Lambda with batch data processing. A function Lambda delay 12 minutes to process a file, but the maximum timeout of Lambda It's 15 The team wants to increase throughput by processing 10 files simultaneously, without a single invocation Lambda try to process all the 10. What is the most appropriate approach??
options: Publish each file as a separate message in SQS and use the Event Source Mapping SQS→Lambda with batch size 1 — o SQS automatically invokes one Lambda by message in parallel, processing up to 10 files simultaneously (limited by competition from Lambda)
Use AWS Step Functions Map state to invoke Lambda in parallel for each file — Map state distributes file array for invocations Lambda independent with up to 40 competing claims
Increase the memory of Lambda for 10.240 MB (maximum) — more memory means more CPU allocated, allowing a single invocation to sue 10 files in parallel threads within the timeout of 15 minutes
Migratory to AWS Fargate with ECS Containers Fargate do not have the limit 15 minutes of Lambda and can process long-term files without timeout restrictions
questions.explanation: Correct. Use SQS with one message per file and batch size=1 in Event Source Mapping does the AWS automatically invoke an instance Lambda by message (in parallel), up to the competition limit set. 10 files in the queue, 10 cases Lambda run competitively — each processing its file by up to 15 minutes. It's the fan-out parallelization pattern with Lambda.
questions.hint: To process multiple files in parallel with Lambda, how to structure the trigger so that each file invokes an instance Lambda independent — which queue service facilitates this fan-out pattern?
optionRationales: Correct. Use SQS with one message per file and batch size=1 in Event Source Mapping does the AWS automatically invoke an instance Lambda by message (in parallel), up to the competition limit set. 10 files in the queue, 10 cases Lambda run competitively — each processing its file by up to 15 minutes. It's the fan-out parallelization pattern with Lambda.

Incorrect for scalability. Lambda allocation CPU proportional to memory, and with more CPU it would be possible to parallel threads within an invocation — but an invocation of 12 minutes per file will not become 1.2 minutes with 10x plus CPU, because processing time per file does not scale linearly with CPU. In addition, it keeps architecture fragile: a failure loses all the 10 files, not just one.

Partially correct: Step Functions Map state is a valid solution for parallel file processing with Lambda. However, for continuous file processing (not a single batch), the approach SQS + Lambda is more suitable — supports new file arrivals dynamically without starting a new workflow Step Functions each batch.

Incorrect as a solution for parallel processing requirement. Fargate is valid if the timeout of 15 minutes is a real limit, but the statement says that 12 minutes is inside the 15 minutes of Lambda. The question is of parallel throughput — that SQS + Lambda elegantly solve without platform migration.

questions.text: A company has a web application that uses Amazon DynamoDB to store inventory data. Queries always filter by ProductCategory AND PriceRange (e.g. 'Electronics with price between R$100 and R$500'). Currently, ProductCategory is the key partition and ProductID is the key lot. The filtered queries by PriceRange result in full scans. How to optimize these queries without creating a new table?
options: Use DynamoDB PartiQL with a SELECT including WHERE ProductCategory = ? AND Price BETWEEN ? AND ? — PartiQL automatically optimizes queries with multiple filters to avoid full scans

Create a Global Secondary Index (GSI) with ProductCategory as partition key and Price as spell key — the GSI allows efficient queries by ProductCategory (equal match) followed by filter by Price (range query in the key spell of GSI), No full scan
Create a Secondary Site Index (LSI) with Price as alternative key spell — or LSI allows you to want in the same key partition (ProductCategory) to efficiently filter by Price as alternative key sort
Add Price as an attribute to the existing key spell (ProductID) using a key compound (ProductID#Price) — you want can then use FilterExpression in both fields simultaneously without additional index
questions.explanation: Right. GSI with ProductCategory as partition key and Price as sort key allows efficient queries: a query specifies ProductCategory (partition key of GSI, exact match) and use BETWEEN/GreaterThan/LessThan at Price GSI, range query). This avoids full scan of the table — the query goes directly to the partition of the GSI for that category and then make range scan in the spell key.
questions.hint: What kind of index is there? DynamoDB can be created at any time (not just in table creation) and use any attribute as partition key and sort key — allowing efficient queries by attribute combinations?
optionRationales: Right. GSI with ProductCategory as partition key and Price as sort key allows efficient queries: a query specifies ProductCategory (partition key of GSI, exact match) and use BETWEEN/GreaterThan/LessThan at Price GSI, range query). This avoids full scan of the table — the query goes directly to the partition of the GSI for that category and then make range scan in the spell key.

Incorrect by technical limitation. Local Secondary Indexes need to use the same PARTITION KEY of the main table (ProductID would be used as partition key of the table, not ProductCategory). If ProductID is the sort key of the table and ProductCategory is the partition key, the LSI would allow filtering by Price within a specific ProductCategory — but LSIs need to have the same partition key. In addition, LSIs need to be created at the time of table creation.

Incorrect. PartiQL is an interface SQL for DynamoDB, but does not change the behavior of access to data — a PartiQL query that filters by attributes without corresponding index still results in a scan table or inefficient query. Optimization comes from creating appropriate indexes (GSI/LSI), not of the used query language.

Incorrect. FilterExpression no DynamoDB does not use indexes — only filters the result AFTER the Query/Scan operation has already been executed. Add Price to the key spell as a composition string would be a change of scheme that would impact all existing operations, and FilterExpression with Price would still not be efficient for range queries without a dedicated key spell via GSI.

questions.text: A company uses Amazon Kinesis Data Streams for IoT event processing. The consumer application needs to process events from each device in order, but different devices can be processed in parallel. The application uses a single function Lambda as a consumer of the stream. How to ensure device sorting and parallelism between devices?
options: Configure multiple functions Lambda (one per device) as consumers of the same stream Kinesis — each Lambda process only the records of your device, ensuring ordination and parallelism
Use the Sequence Number of Kinesis to sort records after processing — the Lambda processes all events in any order and then orders by Sequence Number before persisting
Use SQS FIFO instead of Kinesis — o SQS FIFO ensures ordering by Message Group ID (DeviceID), and messages from different groups are processed in parallel with the Lambda as a consumera

Use DeviceID as a partition key when producing events in Kinesis — o Kinesis ensures that all records with the same partition key go to the same shard, preserving the order per device inside the shard; multiple shards process different devices in parallel
questions.explanation: Correct. Kinesis uses the key partition to determine which shard a record is stored in — all records with the same key partition (DeviceID) go to the same shard and are processed in order within that shard. Different shards process different key partitions in parallel, ensuring parallelism between devices without compromising device sorting.
questions.hint: No. Kinesis, which attribute determines in which shard a record is stored, ensuring that records with the same value are processed in order within a shard?
optionRationales: Correct. Kinesis uses the key partition to determine which shard a record is stored in — all records with the same key partition (DeviceID) go to the same shard and are processed in order within that shard. Different shards process different key partitions in parallel, ensuring parallelism between devices without compromising device sorting.

Partially correct about SQS FIFO: he really guarantees ordination by Message Group ID. But the question asks about Kinesis specifically, and the answer about using partition key is the mechanism DENTRO of the Kinesis to ensure device ordering with parallelism between devices. SQS FIFO would be a change of architecture, not the optimization of Kinesis.

Incorrect and inescalable. With IoT, there may be thousands of devices — having a Lambda by device is unfeasible. In addition, multiple Lambdas consuming the same stream Kinesis do not guarantee that each Lambda process only records of a specific device — all would receive all the stream shards.

Incorrect. Sorting after processing works for events that can be reordered, but for IoT it is common that the ORDEM processing import (e.g. 'open door' must be processed before 'close door' to the same device). Sorting after processing can cause state inconsistencies. The correct design is to ensure that events of the same device are processed sequentially — not randomly followed by correction.

Amazon SageMaker with Elastic Inference — SageMaker Elastic Inference connects acceleration of GPU fractionated to inference instances, reducing the cost of GPU no start cold
Amazon EC2 Spot Instances in one ASG — Spot Instances have lower cost and are available immediately when requested, without cold start

ASG detects the need to scale, Warm Pool instances are promoted for assets much faster than launching new instances — eliminating the cold start of OS and dependencies startup. GPU with slow start time.
questions.hint: What is the functionality of EC2 Auto Scaling keeps pre-initialized instances at a lower cost (stopped or running without traffic), ready for immediate promotion when necessary, eliminating cold start?
optionRationales: Right, Warm Pool of the Auto Scaling keeps pre-initialized instances in the state of stopped (covering only of EBS) or running (normal coverage of EC2 but no traffic). ASG detects the need to scale, Warm Pool instances are promoted for assets much faster than launching new instances — eliminating the cold start of OS and dependencies startup. GPU with slow start time.

Incorrect about removing cold start. Partially correct about Elastic Inference for cost reduction of GPU, but does not solve the cold start. Elastic Inference is an accelerator of GPU fractionated to SageMaker and EC2, not a mechanism for having pre-heated instances. + EC2 GPU is the correct solution for cold start.

questions.text: A company uses Amazon ElasticSearch (OpenSearch Service) to index and search for application logs. With data volume growth, search queries are getting slow. The team realized that most of the queries are looking for only the latest ones. 7 log days, but the index has 2 years of data. Which index management strategy improves the performance of queries without deleting historical data?
options: Implement Index State Management (ISM) with rollover and index transition policies — create indices per day/week (hot tie), after 7 days move to warm tier indices (less shards, lower cost knots), and after 30 days for cold tier (UltraWarm in OpenSearch) or archive in S3, so you wanted the last 7 days only scan recent hot indexes
Using OpenSearch Serverless — has no fixed indexes and automatically scales the demand-based search capability without degradation with increasing data volumes
Enable Request Cache in OpenSearch — frequent queries are cached in the memory of nodes, making the same searches instantly return without re-scanning the index
Increase the number of shards by 5 for 50 — more shards distribute the search load among more us, improving the throughput of wants
questions.explanation: Correct. ISM (Index State Management) at OpenSearch Service allows you to create policies that automatically manage the index life cycle: daily rollover for new indexes, transition to UltraWarm (low cost ter for cold data) after N days, and finally archiving. By separating recent data into dedicated hot indexes, you want the latest 7 days scan only these indices, ignoring years of historical data.
questions.hint: Which feature of OpenSearch Service allows you to create automated policies that move data from 'hot' (recent) indexes to lower cost (cold/filed) third parties based on age?
optionRationales: Correct. ISM (Index State Management) at OpenSearch Service allows you to create policies that automatically manage the index life cycle: daily rollover for new indexes, transition to UltraWarm (low cost ter for cold data) after N days, and finally archiving. By separating recent data into dedicated hot indexes, you want the latest 7 days scan only these indices, ignoring years of historical data.

Incorrect. Increasing shards beyond necessary may PIORAR performance — each shard has overhead management, and with more shards than we available, distributed search efficiency decreases. The problem described is scanning irrelevant historical data, not lack of parallelism. (ISM) is the correct solution.

Partially correct: Request Cache helps with repeated IDENTICAL queries. But logs are usually unique (timestamps, different IDs), so queries are rarely identical — the hit rate cache would be low. In addition, the cache is limited in size and queries from different periods would be constantly cleared. ISM with tiering per period is the correct structural solution.

Incorrect as a direct solution to the problem. OpenSearch Serverless removes the need to provide capacity manually, but still scans TODOS the index data for each query — with 2 years of logs in the same index, the query would still take time proportional to the total volume. The correct solution is to separate indexes by period via ISM to limit the scope of each query.

questions.text: A company uses Amazon SQS with a Standard row and a function Lambda as a consumer. When processing messages, the Lambda often receives the same message multiple times because processing takes longer than the configured Visibility Timeout (30 (seconds). The average processing takes 2 How to solve this without DLQ?
options: Use SQS FIFO with Message Deduplication ID — the deduplication ID ensures that identical messages are not delivered more than once inside a 5 minutes
Enable Long Polling in the queue SQS (WaitTimeSeconds=20) — the long polling ensures that each message is received only once per consumer, eliminating duplicate deliveries.

Increase the Visibility Timeout from the queue SQS for a value greater than the maximum processing time (ex.: 5 minutes) — while the message is being processed, it remains invisible to other consumers for the set period, avoiding duplicate deliveries by timeout
Configure the Lambda to call ChangeMessageVisibility during processing to extend the Visibility Timeout before it expires — this keeps the message invisible while the Lambda Still processing.
questions.explanation: Right. Visibility Timeout should be longer than the maximum processing time of a message. If processing takes 2 minutes, the Visibility Timeout should be at least 3-5 minutes (with safety margin). Lambda is processing, the message remains invisible — only after the full processing and the DeleteMessage is called (or the timeout expires) the message will be available again.
questions.hint: Which row parameter SQS determines how long a message becomes invisible after it is received by a consumer — and what value it should have in relation to processing time?
optionRationales: Right. Visibility Timeout should be longer than the maximum processing time of a message. If processing takes 2 minutes, the Visibility Timeout should be at least 3-5 minutes (with safety margin). Lambda is processing, the message remains invisible — only after the full processing and the DeleteMessage is called (or the timeout expires) the message will be available again.

Incorrect. Long Polling reduces the number of empty chicks and is more efficient than Short Polling (immediate response), but does not solve duplicate deliveries by Visibility Timeout. Long Polling affects the DETECTION of messages in the queue, not the behavior of redelivery by expired timeout.

Partially correct: SQS FIFO with deduplication ID prevents that MENSAGENS IDENTICALS (same content) are added multiple times in a row within 5 minutes — but does not solve the problem of a message being RE-ENTREGUE because Visibility Timeout expired before processing completes. They are different scenarios: deduplication in ENQUEUE vs. redelivered by timeout.

Correct as advanced mechanism (heartbeat visibility), but is not the PRIMEIRA solution to the problem described. Increasing the row's Visibility Timeout to a value appropriate to processing time is the simple and direct solution. ChangeMessageVisibility is useful for processings with variable and unpredictable duration where a fixed timeout is not enough.

questions.text: A company uses AWS Global Accelerator to host an application of online games with ultra-low latency requirements. The team wants to understand the fundamental difference between Global Accelerator and the Amazon CloudFront to choose the correct solution. Global Accelerator uses the private backbone network of AWS (Anycast of static IPs) to route traffic TCP/UDP with more predictable latency for any origin — ideal for non-applications-HTTP (UDP, TCP custom), static IPs required, and endpoint failure; CloudFront is a CDN which caches content in edge locations, optimized for HTTP/S with maximum benefit in cacheable content
Both services are equivalent for web applications — the difference is only cost: Global Accelerator is more expensive per GB of data, while CloudFront is charged by request

CloudFront supports protocols TCP/UDP including WebSockets and gRPC — therefore for online games with low latency requirements, CloudFront is greater than Global Accelerator because it also caches static assets of the game

Global Accelerator provides two static Anycast IPs that route user traffic to the endpoint AWS closer via the private backbone network of the AWS — reducing hops on the public internet. TCP and UDP. Do not cache content. It is ideal for applications that need static IPs, support protocols not-HTTP, or need transparent multi-regional failover. optionRationales: Correct. Global Accelerator provides two static Anycast IPs that route user traffic to the endpoint AWS closer via the private backbone network of the AWS — reducing hops on the public internet. TCP and UDP. Do not cache content. It is ideal for applications that need static IPs, support protocols not-HTTP, or need transparent multi-regional failover. CloudFront is a CDN which caches content HTTP/S in edge locations, with greater benefit for static or cacheable content.

Incorrect. Global Accelerator DO NOT cache content — is a network accelerator, not a CDN. It routed traffic to the nearest backend endpoint via the backbone of AWS, but does not store content in edge locations. CloudFront is the CDN which caches content.

The Global Accelerator supports TCP and UDP, making it more suitable for online games that use custom network protocols based on UDP.

Incorrect. The difference is not just cost — they are fundamentally different services in purpose: Global Accelerator is a network accelerator for TCP/UDP, CloudFront is a CDN for HTTP/S with caching. Using them for the same use cases produces different results in terms of functionality (caching, protocol support, static IPs)).

questions.text: A company uses Amazon DynamoDB to store data from financial transactions. Some critical operations need to ensure that multiple tables are atomically updated — or all writings happen successfully, or none happens (multi-item multi-table atom). What functionality of the DynamoDB You can stand it.?
options: Use DynamoDB Global Tables with synchronous replication between regions — synchronous replication ensures that written in all regions are atomically confirmed before returning to successful application

DynamoDB Conditional Writes with ConditionExpression in each table individually — if the condition fails in any table, the writing is rejected in that table and the application code reverses the writings in the others

DynamoDB Transactions (TransactWriteItems and TransactGetItems) — allow atomic operations on multiple items of multiple tables in the same region AWS; if any operation in the set fails, all are reversed automatically, ensuring atomicity
DynamoDB Streams Lambda Coordination — a Lambda monitors changes in table A via Stream and updates table B in response; if the Lambda fail, Stream allows replay and operation is reprocessed
questions.explanation: Correct. DynamoDB Transactions (using TransactWriteItems and TransactGetItems) provide guarantees ACID for operations in multiple items and multiple tables in the same region. TransactWriteItems accepts up 100 operations (Put, Update, Delete, ConditionCheck) that are performed atomicly — or all are successful, or none is applied. Ideal for financial transactions that need consistency between tables.
questions.hint: Which API of the DynamoDB allows you to perform multiple writing operations (in multiple tables) atomicly — or all happen, or none?
optionRationales: Correct. DynamoDB Transactions (using TransactWriteItems and TransactGetItems) provide guarantees ACID for operations in multiple items and multiple tables in the same region. TransactWriteItems accepts up 100 operations (Put, Update, Delete, ConditionCheck) that are performed atomicly — or all are successful, or none is applied. Ideal for financial transactions that need consistency between tables.

Incorrect. DynamoDB Streams + Lambda is an eventual consistency — non-atomic architecture. Between the writing in table A and the processing of the Stream by Lambda to update Table B, there is a period where the tables are inconsistent. In addition, failures in Lambda can leave permanently drawn tables without complex compensation logic.

Incorrect. Conditional Writes check conditions before CADA individual operation — they are not atomic among multiple tables. If the writing in Table A happens but the condition in Table B fails, the application would need to manually 'undo' Table A with compensation logic — this is complex and prone to errors, especially in case of process failure between the writings. DynamoDB Transactions are designed to eliminate exactly this problem.

Incorrect. DynamoDB Global Tables uses ASSINCRONA replication between regions (possibly consistency cross-region), not synchronous. In addition, Global Tables replicates data from a table to multiple regions — does not provide atomicity between MULTIPLES TABELAS DIFERENTES in the same region, which is the requirement of the.

questions.text: A company uses AWS Direct Connect with a connection of 1 Gbps for data transfer from your data center to AWS. The team realized that the actual throughput hit is of only 600 Mbps due to high round-trip latency (150ms) between sites. Why the throughput TCP is limited even with available bandwidth, and as the Direct Connect can be optimized for this scenario?
options: The Direct Connect does not support speeds above 600 Mbps for connections of 1 Gbps — nominal speed includes protocol overhead, and actual throughput is always ~60% of nominal speed

The problem is the MTU (Maximum Transmission Unit) not optimized — the Direct Connect supports Jumbo Frames (MTU 9001) increase the payload per package; activate Jumbo Frames in ENIs of instances EC2 increases the throughput to the maximum available

The Throughput TCP is limited by bandwidth-delay product (BDP = bandwidth × RTT) — with 150more than RTT and window size standard of 64KB, the theoretical maximum throughput is ~430Kbps per flow TCP; to use the whole band of Direct Connect, multiple flows are required TCP parallel or tune o TCP window size in instances EC2 (stairs receiving windows)

The limit of 600 Mbps is a limitation of Direct Connect Standard — to achieve 1 Gbps of actual throughput, it is necessary to hire the Direct Connect Dedicated Connection Boost that increases effective throughput
questions.explanation: Correct. TCP Bandwidth-Delay Product (BDP) defines how much data may be 'on flight' without confirmation: BDP = bandwidth × RTT. With 150ms RTT and window size of 64KB, flow throughput TCP It's ~3.4 Mbps — far below 1 Gbps. To saturated the band, TCP window size needs to be at least BDP = 1Gbps × 0.15s = 150 Mbit = ~18.75 MB. Multiple parallel streams or window size tuning (tcp window scaling) solve that. Direct Connect reduces latency but does not eliminate the problem of BDP.
questions.hint: The Throughput TCP in high latency connections is limited by the 'bandwidth-delay product' — the window TCP must be large enough to keep the line full. What is the formula and what needs to be adjusted?
optionRationales: Correct. TCP Bandwidth-Delay Product (BDP) defines how much data may be 'on flight' without confirmation: BDP = bandwidth × RTT. With 150ms RTT and window size of 64KB, flow throughput TCP It's ~3.4 Mbps — far below 1 Gbps. To saturated the band, TCP window size needs to be at least BDP = 1Gbps × 0.15s = 150 Mbit = ~18.75 MB. Multiple parallel streams or window size tuning (tcp window scaling) solve that. Direct Connect reduces latency but does not eliminate the problem of BDP.

Incorrect. There is no 'Direct Connect Boost' as a separate product. The throughput limit is determined by the speed of the contracted door (1 Gbps, 10 Gbps, 100 Gbps) and by network factors such as BDP, not by an arbitrary limitation of the product which can be 'unlocked''.

Incorrect. There's no such thing '60% Overhead' fixed. Effective throughput depends on network factors (window TCP, RTT, number of flows), not of a product limitation. TCP window size and RTT appropriate, it is possible to approach 100% of nominal door speed Direct Connect.

Partially correct: Jumbo Frames (MTU 9001) reduces the overhead header by data byte and can improve throughput in high latency links — but is not the main cause of the problem described. BDP (bandwidth-delay product) is the primary limiting factor, and Jumbo Frames itself do not compensate for the limitation of TCP window size 150more than RTT.

questions.text: A company stores 500 TB historical backups no Amazon S3 Standard. The recoveries are by GB recovered, but with rare access, the total cost is much lower than S3 Standard. Meets the requirement for restoration in 1-2 hours — in practice in milliseconds.

S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval has instant retrieval with lower cost of retrieval than Flexible Retrieval Expedited.

Incorrect about 'no recovery charge''. S3 Standard-IA TEM Retriival Collection by GB — this is one of its features (storage cheaper, retriival more expensive). 500 TB with rare but urgent access, Standard-IA offers less storage economy than Glacier Instant Retrieval (~57% vs ~68% of economy), and also has retrieval collection. Glacier Instant Retrieval is more economical for this profile.

Incorrect. S3 Glacier Deep Archive has recovery time from 12 hours (Standard) or 48 hours (Bulk) — DOES NOT meet the restoration requirement in 1-2 The Bulk/Standard emergency recovery is not within the SLA of 2 hours. Glacier Instant Retrieval is the right choice for rare data with urgent recovery requirement.

questions.text: A company uses Amazon EC2 with Auto Scaling for a batch data processing application. Batch jobs are started at 9h and finished at 17h, from Monday to Friday. Outside this time, the instances become idle. The team wants to reduce costs without compromising the availability of processing during business hours. MAIS economic for this use profile?
options: EC2 Scheduled Reserved Instances or Auto Scaling with Scheduled Actions (scale-in to 0 outside the time + scale-out for the necessary capacity to 9(h) using Spot Instances for batch workers — Spot Instance with Spot Diversified Fleet reduces costs by up to 90% and Scheduled Actions avoid idle instances out of time
Use smaller (downsize) instances that run 24/7 instead of big instances that get idle out of time
Migrate batch workload to AWS Lambda with Scheduled Events — Lambda charge only for the execution time (thousands of seconds), without cost to idle instances
Reserved Instances Standard with 1 end year for all batch instances — ensure 40% discount on On-Demand even for out-of-time instances
questions.explanation: Correct. For batch jobs with predictable schedule, Scheduled Actions no ASG combined with Spot Instances for batch workers (tolerating interruption — restartable processing) offer maximum economy: Spot reduces cost by up to 90% about On-Demand, and Scheduled Actions guarantee 0 instances outside working hours (8h * 5 days = 40h use by 168h weekly = ~24% of use, making RIs less efficient than On-Demand with Scheduled Actions).
questions.hint: For predictable batch jobs that only run on business hours, which combination eliminates cost of idle instances and uses the maximum discount for workloads tolerant of interruption?
optionRationales: Correct. For batch jobs with predictable schedule, Scheduled Actions no ASG combined with Spot Instances for batch workers (tolerating interruption — restartable processing) offer maximum economy: Spot reduces cost by up to 90% about On-Demand, and Scheduled Actions guarantee 0 instances outside working hours (8h * 5 days = 40h use by 168h weekly = ~24% of use, making RIs less efficient than On-Demand with Scheduled Actions).

Incorrect. Reserved Instances Standard charge CONTINUAMENTE by the term — not only when the instance is running. Pay by 168weekly RI for use only 40h (24% of time) is not economical. EC2 Stopped state still charge RI fees in Standard RIs. Use On-Demand with Scheduled Actions (paying only 40h/week) + Spot It would be much cheaper..

Incorrect. Reducing the size to save in idle capacity results in slower batch jobs (less CPU/I would also like to pay for 24/7 with smaller instances instead of 40h/week with correct size instances. Turn off completely out of time + Spot is economically superior.

Incorrect for heavy batch workloads. Lambda has a limit of 15 minutes by invocation and is not suitable for data processing jobs that run for hours. Long-term batch jobs need to EC2, ECS, or AWS Batch — no Lambda. In addition, Lambda has memory limits (10GB) which may be insufficient for large-scale data processing.

questions.text: A company stores log data in Amazon S3 and use the Amazon Athena for analysis. The account AWS The team found out that the Lambda processing the results of the Athena is in a different region of the pocket S3. What change would eliminate these cross-region transfer costs?
